title: Ancient Greece in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the main eras of ancient Greece from the Bronze Age to Roman rule.
summary: Greek history runs from Bronze Age palaces (to about 1200 BCE) through a Dark Age, the Archaic, Classical and Hellenistic ages, to Roman rule.

cards.headline: Ancient Greece wasn’t one moment. It was a relay race of eras.
cards.body: Palace kingdoms, a dark age, city-states and colonies, then Rome. Here’s the whole track before we run it lap by lap.

mascot.line: You don’t need every date on this timeline. Remember the order of the five eras.

events.label: Bronze Age: palace kingdoms on Crete, then on the mainland
Dark Age: the palace kingdoms are gone
Archaic age: city-states grow and colonies spread
Classical age, ending with Alexander the Great’s death
Hellenistic age: Greek kingdoms, until Rome takes Egypt

cards.headline: The famous part came late
cards.body: Picture ancient Greece and you probably see the Classical age, 480 to 323 BCE: the Greece of the postcards. But the Bronze Age palaces had fallen roughly 700 years before it began. So that famous stretch is less than 160 years of a story that runs for well over a thousand. It’s like summing up your whole family history with last summer’s vacation photos.

cards.fact: Rome conquered mainland Greece in 146 BCE.
cards.context: That year a Roman army defeated the Greek Achaean League and destroyed the city of Corinth. The Greek kingdoms farther east held out a little longer: the last, Egypt, fell to Rome in 30 BCE. That’s the finish line. This chapter starts back at the very beginning, with palaces, myths and memory.

title: Mountains and Sea
objective: After this level you can explain how mountains and the sea shaped Greek life.
summary: Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece and split communities apart, while the sea was never far off and became the easiest road.

cards.headline: In Greece, the sea is never far away. Your neighbors often were.
cards.body: Mountains made the walk next door hard work, and the sea opened the way to far-off places. That odd combination shaped Greek life.

mascot.line: Hold on to these mountains. Level 11 uses them to explain why Greece had so many cities.

cards.headline: A land of mountains
cards.body: Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece. They made travel over land hard, so communities in separate valleys grew up apart and developed independently. Athens and Thebes sit less than 100 km (60 miles) apart, yet they came to see each other as foreign rivals. Imagine the next town over treating you like a foreigner. In Greece, that was normal.

cards.headline: Never far from the sea
cards.body: Now look at the coastline. Arms of the sea reach so deep into the land that only a small wedge of the interior is more than 80 km (50 miles) from the coast. Today’s Greece also counts more than 2,000 islands. Mountains blocked travel over land, but the sea opened up wider horizons. For a Greek, the easiest road was usually water.

cards.fact: Only about one-fifth of Greece is lowland.
cards.context: Lowland is the best farmland, and in Greece there was never much of it. Picture a town boxed in by mountains, with only a small patch of good fields. Hold on to that picture: it comes back in Level 9.

title: The Minoans
objective: After this level you can describe the palace culture of Minoan Crete.
summary: Arthur Evans dug Knossos on Crete from 1900, named its Bronze Age builders Minoans after King Minos, and rebuilt parts of the palace in concrete.

cards.headline: Greek myth put a monster in a maze on Crete. In 1900, a man went digging.
cards.body: He found a palace instead, and he gave a lost civilization the name it still goes by.

cards.headline: The palace at Knossos
cards.body: The myth: King Minos of Crete kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus. In 1900 the British archaeologist Arthur Evans began digging at Knossos, on Crete, and uncovered a great palace. Its twisting maze of rooms and corridors led some archaeologists to link it with the Labyrinth, though many now doubt it. A maze-like palace, right where the myth put the maze: you can see why the idea stuck.

cards.headline: Named after a myth
cards.body: Evans named the people who built the palace Minoans, after the legendary King Minos. The name is his, not theirs. Their own writing, a script called Linear A, has never been deciphered, so their records can’t speak for them. A whole civilization goes by a nickname borrowed from Greek myth.

cards.headline: A culture of sea and color
cards.body: The Minoans flourished on Crete from about 3000 BCE to about 1100 BCE. They traded across the Aegean and with Egypt and the Levant; remember Level 2’s sea road? Their palace walls were painted with dancing, sports and dolphins. By the mid-15th century BCE their palace culture was in decline, as influence from mainland Greece grew. Hold that thought for Level 4.

cards.headline: Rebuilt in concrete
cards.body: From the 1920s, Evans’s team rebuilt parts of the palace in reinforced concrete, and his artists completed its wall paintings from fragments. The philosopher R. G. Collingwood joked that the rebuilt architecture seemed to consist of garages and public lavatories. So walk Knossos with care: part of what you see is ancient, and part is Evans’s best guess.

title: The Mycenaeans
objective: After this level you can describe the Mycenaean warrior kingdoms.
summary: Mycenaean kings ruled from fortified palaces; their Linear B tablets, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, are the oldest written Greek.

cards.headline: The oldest Greek anyone can read turned out to be paperwork.
cards.body: No songs of heroes, just palace records. Cracking them in 1952 still changed what we know about early Greece.

cards.headline: Warrior kings of the mainland
cards.body: On the Greek mainland, the Bronze Age belonged to the Mycenaeans. Their kings ruled from fortified palaces at places like Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns. The walls were built of stones so huge that later Greeks called them Cyclopean, believing only the one-eyed giants, the Cyclopes, could have moved them. When people credit your walls to giants, you built well.

cards.headline: A mask for a king who wasn’t there
cards.body: In 1876 Heinrich Schliemann dug into a grave at Mycenae and found a gold funerary mask. He believed it belonged to Agamemnon, the king of Mycenae who, in legend, led the Greeks against Troy. It doesn’t: the mask dates to about 1550–1500 BCE, roughly 300 years before Agamemnon would have lived, if he existed. The name stuck anyway. It’s still the Mask of Agamemnon.

cards.headline: Cracking Linear B
cards.body: The Mycenaean palaces kept records on clay tablets in a script called Linear B. In 1952 a British architect, Michael Ventris, working with John Chadwick, deciphered it and showed it was an early form of Greek: the oldest known written Greek. The tablets, from about 1400 to 1200 BCE, were used to run the palaces, mostly as inventories. The oldest Greek you can read is, basically, a stockroom list.

cards.fact: Linear B tablets turned up at Knossos, too.
cards.context: They were found on Crete as well as at Pylos, Mycenae and other mainland palaces. Remember Level 3’s Minoans, declining as influence from the mainland grew? Records in Greek inside the palace of Minos fit that story.

title: The Trojan War
objective: After this level you can explain what legend and archaeology tell us about Troy.
summary: Legend tells of a ten-year siege of Troy. Troy was real, at Hisarlik in Turkey, and Troy VIIa fell around 1200 BCE, but the war as told may be legend.

cards.headline: Was the Trojan War real? Troy was. The war is a harder question.
cards.body: First the legend, then what the spades found, and then where the two meet.

cards.headline: The story Greeks told
cards.body: In legend, Paris, a prince of Troy, took Helen, the wife of Menelaus. A Greek army led by Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, sailed after them and besieged Troy for ten years. Later Greek writers dated the war to the 12th or 13th century BCE. It’s the ultimate family feud: one runaway couple, ten years of war.

cards.fact: The wooden horse isn’t in the Iliad.
cards.context: Homer’s great war poem never shows it. The horse is mentioned in the Odyssey and told in full in Virgil’s Aeneid. The most famous trick of the Trojan War is missing from the most famous poem about it.

cards.headline: Digging for Troy
cards.body: Troy was real. Its ruins lie at Hisarlik, in northwestern Turkey near the Dardanelles. Frank Calvert dug there first and persuaded Heinrich Schliemann, who excavated on a large scale from 1870. Schliemann was sure Homer’s Troy lay at the bottom of the mound. But the mound holds nine main layers, Troy I to Troy IX, and the gold he called “Priam’s Treasure” came from Troy II, about a thousand years too early.

mascot.line: People blur these two all the time: Troy was real, but the ten-year war is unproven.

cards.headline: So, was it real?
cards.body: Scholars point to Troy VI or Troy VIIa as the city behind the legend, and Troy VIIa was destroyed around 1200 BCE, close to where later Greeks placed the war. Still, archaeology suggests a conflict on the scale of Homer’s ten-year siege may never have happened. The honest answer: a real city, a real destruction, and a legend wrapped around them whose size nobody can confirm.

title: Homer
objective: After this level you can describe Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and why Greeks learned them by heart.
summary: The Iliad covers weeks of the Trojan War; the Odyssey, a ten-year journey home. They were the core of Greek education, and who composed them is still debated.

cards.headline: A dinner guest in ancient Greece could recite all of Homer. His dad made him.
cards.body: In Xenophon’s Symposium, Niceratus says his father had him learn the Iliad and Odyssey by heart so he’d grow up to be a good man. Why these two poems?

cards.headline: Two epics, two journeys
cards.body: The Iliad covers just a few weeks in the final year of the Trojan War. It centers on the anger of Achilles and ends with the funeral of Hector, before Troy falls. The Odyssey follows Odysseus, king of Ithaca, who spends 10 years trying to get home after the war. One poem is about a war that won’t end; the other is about a man who can’t get home.

cards.headline: Greece’s textbook
cards.body: For Greeks, these were far more than stories. Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education and culture throughout the Classical age. That’s why Niceratus’s father set the whole of Homer as homework. If you wanted your son to grow up good, Homer was the textbook.

cards.headline: Who was Homer?
cards.body: Homer is thought to have lived in the 9th or 8th century BCE, if he was a single poet at all. That’s the Homeric question, and it’s still open. Some scholars think one poet composed both epics; others think many people retold and revised them. Either way, the poems grew out of a centuries-old oral tradition: singers inherited phrases, scenes and plots and reshaped them each time they performed.

cards.headline: Singing without writing
cards.body: In the 1930s the scholar Milman Parry showed how that could work. Homer repeats set phrases such as “swift-footed Achilles”: building blocks a singer could use while composing on the spot. In Yugoslavia, Parry recorded singers, including one who could not read, performing an epic about as long as the Odyssey. No page, no problem.

title: The Greek Dark Age
objective: After this level you can explain what happened after the Bronze Age palaces fell.
summary: Around 1200 BCE the Mycenaean palaces fell in a wider collapse with debated causes. Writing was lost and population fell, but Lefkandi shows life went on.

cards.headline: Around 1200 BCE, the palaces fell and Greece stopped writing.
cards.body: For about four centuries, no written records survive. So what brought the palaces down, and how do we know anything about the silence that followed?

cards.headline: A whole world breaks
cards.body: The fall wasn’t only Greek. Around 1200 BCE, collapse swept the eastern Mediterranean: the Mycenaean palaces fell, and so did the great Hittite Empire. The suspects include earthquakes, drought and raiders known as the Sea Peoples. No single cause explains it all, so many historians picture several blows landing at once. Think dominoes: you don’t need one giant push if every piece is already wobbling.

cards.headline: Why “dark”?
cards.body: Remember Level 4? Linear B was palace bookkeeping. With the palaces gone, writing was lost, and no written accounts from the next centuries survive. Population fell, and many settlements were abandoned. Even the metal changed: bronze needed long-distance trade, but iron could be mined in Greece, so iron came to replace it. “Dark” mostly means we can’t read about this age.

cards.headline: A light in the dark
cards.body: At Lefkandi, on the island of Euboea, archaeologists found a grave from about 1000 BCE that is rich by the standards of any period. Inside a large building lay gold and a bronze vessel from Cyprus. Somebody in the “Dark Age” had overseas connections and serious wealth. That’s why historians now think the age was less dark than once believed: Greek culture and trade carried on.

title: The Greek Alphabet
objective: After this level you can explain how the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet.
summary: Greeks borrowed the Phoenician alphabet by the 8th century BCE and turned five consonant letters into vowels. It’s the ancestor of European alphabets.

cards.headline: Try reading this: THS SNTNC HS N VWLS.
cards.body: You probably managed, with a little guessing. The alphabet the Greeks borrowed worked like that: no vowels. They fixed it.

cards.headline: Letters from the Phoenicians
cards.body: In the 8th century BCE at the latest, and probably earlier, the Greeks borrowed an alphabet from the Phoenicians, whom they met through trade. It had letters only for consonants; readers filled in the vowels themselves. Remember Level 7? Greece had lost writing when the palaces fell. Now writing came back, by way of the traders.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: the Greeks added the vowels.

cards.headline: Old letters, new jobs
cards.body: The Greeks’ big change was vowels. They took five Phoenician consonant letters and gave them new jobs: aleph became alpha, he became epsilon, yod became iota, ayin became omicron and waw became upsilon. Even the name survives: alphabet comes from alpha and beta, which go back to Phoenician aleph, “ox”, and beth, “house”. Every time you say alphabet, you’re saying “ox, house”.

cards.headline: A prize for the best dancer
cards.body: The earliest datable Greek alphabet inscriptions, from about 725 BCE, come from Athens and from a Greek colony on Ischia, an island off Italy. The one from Athens is scratched on a wine jug, and it names the jug as a prize for the best dancer. So one of the first things Greeks wrote in their new letters was a party trophy.

cards.fact: You’re reading the Greek alphabet’s descendants right now.
cards.context: The Greek alphabet is the direct or indirect ancestor of all modern European alphabets, including the Latin letters of this sentence and Cyrillic.

title: Colonies Around the Sea
objective: After this level you can explain why Greeks founded colonies from Spain to the Black Sea.
summary: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE, Greeks short of land and resources founded independent colonies, from Marseille to the Black Sea.

cards.headline: Plato said people lived around the sea “like ants or frogs about a pond.”
cards.body: He meant his world, from Gibraltar to the Black Sea, and he had a point: Greek towns ringed the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. How did the frogs get all the way around the pond?

cards.headline: Why leave home?
cards.body: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE, Greeks founded new cities along the coasts of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Why go? Remember Level 2’s thin slice of lowland: as populations grew, towns ran short of farmland. Greece also lacked metals, timber and grain, and quarrels at home pushed people out. Trade usually came first, and settlers followed.

cards.headline: A new city, not a branch office
cards.body: A colony was founded by a mother city, but it didn’t take orders from it. Colonies were politically independent, though they modeled themselves on the cities that founded them. Think of a grown child moving out: same family habits, own front door.

cards.headline: From Sicily to France
cards.body: Corinth founded Syracuse, on Sicily, in 733 BCE. Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia about 600 BCE; today it’s Marseille. So many Greek cities rose along southern Italy’s coast that the region was called Magna Graecia, “Great Greece”. The first, on the island of Ischia and at Cumae, date to about 750 BCE. Ischia? That’s where Level 8’s early inscription turned up.

title: The Polis
objective: After this level you can explain what a Greek city-state was.
summary: A polis was an independent town plus its countryside; there were over a thousand, most of them small, and the word lives on in “politics”.

cards.headline: Ancient Greece had no capital city. It had more than a thousand cities.
cards.body: No single king, no one government, no national flag. So what exactly was a Greek city, and why were there so many?

mascot.line: Keep this picture: a town, its fields and its own government. That’s a polis.

cards.headline: A town with its farms attached
cards.body: The Greek word is polis, usually translated “city-state”. A polis was a town plus the countryside for some miles around, villages and all. Picture your town, the farms beyond it, and a line where the next town’s fields begin. Now give that town its own government. Each polis was independent of its neighbors, and the Greek city-states never formed a permanent union.

cards.headline: Small by design
cards.body: Scholars have catalogued 1,035 Greek city-states, out of some 1,500 in all. Most were tiny by our standards: several hundred to a couple of thousand people, closer to a big school than a big city. The island of Lesbos alone held five of them. Imagine five countries sharing one island, each sure it was the best.

cards.headline: Why so many?
cards.body: Remember Level 2? Mountains made travel hard, so communities in separate valleys grew up apart and independently. The polis emerged around 750 BCE and stayed the main way Greeks organized themselves until the Roman Empire. It still lives in your vocabulary: politics comes from Greek politikos, “of citizens”, from polis. Talk politics and you’re talking city-state business.

title: Acropolis and Agora
objective: After this level you can describe the high city and the marketplace.
summary: A Greek town had a fortified high city, the acropolis, for refuge and temples, and an open agora for politics, trials, worship and trade.

cards.headline: Every Greek town had two hearts: one up high, one down low.
cards.body: One was for safety and the gods. The other was for shopping, arguing and gossip. Meet the acropolis and the agora.

cards.headline: The high city
cards.body: Acropolis means “high city”. It was the town’s fortified high ground: the place to run to when enemies came, and home to its chief temples. Some were old strongholds. Remember Level 4’s palace kings? The Mycenaeans built a palace on the Acropolis of Athens. Think of it as the town’s castle and cathedral rolled into one.

cards.headline: The meeting place
cards.body: Down below lay the agora, an open space where citizens met for nearly everything: worship, politics, trials, business and plain socializing. Covered colonnades called stoas often ran along its edges, some with shops inside. Town square, mall and courthouse, all at once. The word survives in agoraphobia, the fear of open spaces, coined in 1871 from agora.

cards.headline: A stone that talks
cards.body: How do we know where Athens’ Agora ended? The stones tell us, literally. Around 500 BCE, Athenians set marble boundary stones at its edges, inscribed “I am the boundary of the Agora.” No arrows, no fine print: just a rock introducing itself. Handy, if a little chatty.

title: Kings, Tyrants and the Few
objective: After this level you can compare the kinds of government in Greek cities.
summary: Greek cities were ruled by kings, aristocrats, oligarchs or tyrants; a tyrant seized power but wasn’t necessarily cruel, like Cypselus of Corinth.

cards.headline: Corinth’s first tyrant ruled without a bodyguard.
cards.body: He was that popular. So why do we call him a tyrant? Because Greek words for government didn’t mean quite what ours do.

mascot.line: Careful: a Greek tyrant seized power. That didn’t automatically make him cruel.

cards.headline: What made a tyrant
cards.body: A king inherited power. A Greek tyrant seized it. In the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, tyrants took over many city-states by rallying people fed up with rule by a few aristocrats. The title didn’t automatically mean cruel: Greeks judged a tyrant by how he ruled. Even the word was an import, probably borrowed from Lydian, a language of Asia Minor.

cards.headline: The Corinth story
cards.body: In the 8th and early 7th centuries BCE, an aristocratic family, the Bacchiads, ruled Corinth, and they founded colonies including Syracuse. They also ruled violently. Around 657 BCE, Cypselus overthrew them, with popular support and a favorable oracle from Delphi. Then he governed without a bodyguard. Rule by the few, then rule by one: same city, new system.

title: Citizens and Outsiders
objective: After this level you can explain who counted as a citizen and who did not.
summary: Citizenship came by birth; only men had political rights. Metics, free resident foreigners, paid a special tax, needed a sponsor and rarely became citizens.

cards.headline: You could live in a Greek city all your life and still be a foreigner.
cards.body: So could your children, and theirs. Paying taxes and working there didn’t make you belong. Birth did.

cards.headline: Citizens: born, not made
cards.body: A citizen belonged to the polis: he could vote, and he owed it taxes and military service. Citizenship normally came by birth to citizen parents, and outsiders were only rarely granted it, even after generations. Only men had political rights, though women still counted as citizens legally, socially and religiously. Membership ran in families, like a surname.

cards.headline: Metics: the neighbors who stayed
cards.body: Most Greek states had metics: free resident foreigners, including freed slaves. The word comes from metoikos, “one who has changed his residence”. Athens had the most. There a metic paid a yearly tax, 12 drachmas for a man, and needed a citizen sponsor. He couldn’t own land or a house without a special grant. The law protected metics, but they always stood a step outside.

cards.fact: Pasion, a former slave, became a great banker in Athens as a metic.
cards.context: He built his fortune in 4th-century BCE Athens, and the city later granted him citizenship. That was the rare exception: most metic families stayed metics, however long they lived there.

title: Slavery in Greece
objective: After this level you can explain the role of slavery in Greek cities.
summary: Slaves, mostly war captives and people seized by raiders, were legal property and did every kind of work, worst of all in the mines; freed slaves became metics.

cards.headline: In some Greek cities, up to a third of the people were owned by someone else.
cards.body: The same city-states that prized the free citizen ran on enslaved labor. It’s the other half of the story, and it deserves to be told plainly.

cards.headline: How people were enslaved
cards.body: War was the main road into slavery: captives could be sold. Pirates and raiders seized non-Greeks to the north and east and sold them in Greece. Greeks enslaved Greeks defeated in war too, just not members of their own polis. Chattel slavery spread after about 600 BCE. By law a slave was property: Aristotle called a slave “a live article of property”.

cards.headline: Every kind of work
cards.body: Enslaved people cooked, cleaned, fetched water, farmed, and worked beside potters and metalworkers. The worst fate was the mines: narrow tunnels, prone to landslides. The silver mines at Laurium, in Athens’ territory, used as many as 30,000 slaves. Some slaves belonged to the city itself: in Athens, public slaves certified that the city’s coins were genuine.

cards.headline: Free, but not a citizen
cards.body: Some slaves did win their freedom. Remember Level 14’s metics? A freed slave joined them: free to live and work in the city, but still not a citizen. Pasion made that journey from slave to banker. Freedom was one border crossed. Citizenship was another border altogether.

title: Hoplites and the Phalanx
objective: After this level you can explain how armored citizens fought shoulder to shoulder.
summary: Hoplites, citizens who bought their own armor, fought in a phalanx about eight ranks deep, each sheltering behind his neighbor’s shield.

cards.headline: Greek armies marching into battle drifted to the right. All of them.
cards.body: The historian Thucydides noticed it and explained why. The answer lies in how Greek citizens fought: packed together, shield beside shield.

cards.headline: The hoplite
cards.body: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier: metal helmet, breastplate, greaves on his shins, a shield on his left forearm, a sword, and a thrusting spear about 2 m (6 ft) long. Hoplites appeared probably in the late 8th century BCE. Remember Level 14: citizens owed military service. Hoplites paid for their own gear, so only men of some property could serve.

cards.headline: The phalanx
cards.body: Hoplites marched shoulder to shoulder in a rectangular block called a phalanx, normally eight ranks deep. Holding the line was everything. The poet Archilochus, in the 7th century BCE, praised a soldier who is “a short man firmly placed upon his legs”, not to be uprooted from his spot. Forget solo heroics: this was teamwork with spears.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: in a phalanx, your safety was your neighbor’s shield.

cards.headline: Why the drift?
cards.body: Here’s Thucydides’ answer. The shield sat on the left arm, so each man’s right side was exposed. Nervous, he edged right to shelter behind the shield of the man beside him, and the whole block crept sideways. Your safety depended on your neighbor, and his on you. Hard to picture a better lesson in being a citizen.

title: Coins and Trade
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek cities began minting coins.
summary: Coins began in Lydia; Greek cities then minted their own, each with its own emblem, and the obol and drachma recall older spit-money.

cards.headline: Greek pocket change started out as kitchen skewers.
cards.body: Before coins, Greeks used metal spits as money. Here’s how cities went from skewers to silver stamped with their own badges.

cards.headline: Born next door
cards.body: The first coins were made in Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the second half of the 7th century BCE. They were electrum, a mix of gold and silver. Remember Level 13’s tyrant, a word probably borrowed from Lydian? Money came from the same neighborhood. A lump of precious metal with an official stamp: simple, portable, and nothing to roast.

cards.headline: Skewers and handfuls
cards.body: The names remember what came before. The small coin called an obol takes its name from obelos, “spit”. Six obols made a drachma, a name that probably meant “a handful”, from a Greek word for grasp. So a drachma was, originally, a fistful of skewers. Your pocket change once doubled as a barbecue set.

cards.headline: Money as a flag
cards.body: Each city-state stamped its own identity on its coins. Aegina’s silver showed a sea turtle, a symbol of its naval strength. Athens’ “owls” were struck from Laurium silver and circulated throughout the Classical world. Aegina’s later coins show a land tortoise, which the Art Institute of Chicago reads as sea power lost to Athens. And in Athens, public slaves checked that coins were genuine.

title: The Olympic Games
objective: After this level you can describe the ancient Olympics and the truce that protected them.
summary: Every four years Greeks met at Olympia to honor Zeus; the first event was a single sprint, winners got olive wreaths, and a truce guaranteed safe travel.

cards.headline: The first Olympic champion on record was a cook.
cards.body: Coroebus of Elis won the sprint in 776 BCE. After that, Greeks from rival city-states met every four years to race, and, remarkably, to hold their fire.

cards.headline: One race to start
cards.body: The Games were held every four years at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus. At first there was a single event, the stadion: a sprint of one length of the track, about 192 m (210 yards). Yes, it gave us the word stadium. Winners got no money, just a wreath of wild olive leaves. Bragging rights did the rest.

cards.headline: Who got in
cards.body: The Games were panhellenic: open to all Greeks, not just one city. In practice, that meant freeborn Greek men, who competed naked. Married women were not allowed to attend. So “all Greeks” meant some Greeks, a pattern you’ll recognize from Level 14.

cards.headline: A truce with teeth
cards.body: Getting to Olympia could mean crossing enemy land. So a truce of several weeks let athletes and spectators travel safely, even while wars went on. It wasn’t world peace; it was a safe road. And it was enforced. Thucydides reports that in 420 BCE Sparta was barred from the Games for sending hoplites into Lepreum during the truce, and fined two minae per soldier.

title: The Oracle at Delphi
objective: After this level you can explain how the Oracle advised cities and kings.
summary: At Delphi the Pythia spoke for Apollo; colonists, cities and kings consulted her, and her ambiguous answers could mislead, as Croesus learned.

cards.headline: A king asked Delphi about war. The answer was true, and it ruined him.
cards.body: That’s the story of Croesus and the Greek world’s great advice service. Cities, colonists and kings all lined up to ask.

cards.headline: Ask Apollo
cards.body: At Delphi, in the mountains of central Greece, a prophetess called the Pythia spoke the will of the god Apollo, seated on a sacred tripod. The oracle worked only a limited number of days, and generous donors could jump to the head of the line. Even divine advice, it turns out, had a VIP queue.

cards.headline: Advice for cities
cards.body: Greeks planning a new colony most often asked Apollo at Delphi for approval first. Remember Level 9’s colonies? Delphi’s blessing was part of the send-off. And in Level 13, Cypselus took Corinth with a favorable oracle from Delphi. A yes from Apollo was a powerful thing to have on your side.

mascot.line: Delphi’s answers were often ambiguous. Lesson: always ask a follow-up question.

cards.headline: Read the small print
cards.body: Priests wrote the answers down in verse that was often highly ambiguous. Herodotus tells how Croesus of Lydia, the kingdom that made the first coins, asked whether to attack Persia. He would destroy a great empire, came the reply. He attacked, and the empire he destroyed was his own. Treat it as a story Greeks loved to tell, not a transcript.

title: Checkpoint: City-States

summary: Over a thousand independent city-states, each with its own rulers, citizens and coins, still saw themselves as one people through language, gods, Olympia and Delphi.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: over a thousand independent cities. One people?

cards.headline: What split them, what joined them

items.label: What split them
points: Their own coins and patron gods

items.label: What joined them
points: A shared language, religion and culture

cards.headline: In their own words
cards.body: Herodotus gives us a Greek definition of being Greek. In his history, the Athenians say all Greeks share kinship in blood and speech, shrines and sacrifices, and a like way of life. Notice what’s missing: a king, a capital, a single government. Greece was a family of cities, not a country.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 2 together. Mountains helped make small, independent city-states, each with a high citadel and a busy agora. Some were ruled by a few aristocrats, some by tyrants. Citizens, by birth, voted, paid taxes and fought, while metics and slaves stood outside. Each city stamped its own coins, yet all could meet at Olympia under a truce and ask Apollo at Delphi.

title: Athens
objective: After this level you can describe Athens and its patron goddess, Athena.
summary: The Greeks told that Athena won Athens with an olive tree. Athens ruled all of Attica and honored her with the owl and the Panathenaia.

cards.headline: The Greeks said Athens got its goddess by holding a contest.
cards.body: Two gods wanted the city. One offered water, the other a tree. Guess which gift won, and why Athens never forgot it.

cards.headline: A spring or a tree?
cards.body: Here’s the myth. Poseidon, god of the sea, struck a rock and made a spring, but its water was salty. (In some versions he offered the first horse instead.) Athena planted the first olive tree. Her gift won, and the city took her name: Athens. A salty spring against olives, oil and shade? Not a hard call.

cards.headline: One city, a whole region
cards.body: Remember Level 2: mountains split Greece into valleys that grew up apart. Athens broke the pattern. It ruled the whole region of Attica, an area remarkably large for one city-state; it could have held several. Athenian myth said the hero Theseus had united Attica’s towns. By the fifth century BCE, citizens from every corner of Attica were Athenians, with the same rights and duties.

cards.headline: The goddess’s birthday party
cards.body: Athens never let the story go. Athena’s little owl became the city’s symbol. Every July, the Panathenaia festival celebrated her birthday and presented the goddess with a new embroidered robe; every fourth year it was held with great splendor. Winners at its games took home jars painted with Athena and filled with olive oil from her sacred trees. The prize for beating everyone? A jar of the goddess’s own gift.

title: Solon's Reforms
objective: After this level you can explain how Solon eased debt and changed the laws.
summary: About 594 BCE Solon cancelled debts and freed Athenians enslaved for debt, replaced Draco’s harsh code, and ranked citizens by wealth instead of birth.

cards.headline: In early Athens, an unpaid debt could make you a slave.
cards.body: Poor Athenians borrowed against their own bodies, and some were sold abroad. Around 594 BCE, one man was handed the job of fixing it.

cards.headline: Shaking off the burdens
cards.body: Before Solon, a poor Athenian could borrow with his own person as security. If he couldn’t pay, he could be enslaved, even sold abroad. Solon, archon (chief official) about 594 BCE, cancelled debts, freed the enslaved debtors and banned loans secured on a person. Athenians called it the “shaking off of burdens.” In a poem, Solon boasted of bringing home many who had been sold into slavery.

cards.fact: “Draconian” comes from Draco, whose laws punished even trivial crimes with death.
cards.context: Draco gave Athens that code around 621 BCE. Solon replaced it, keeping only Draco’s laws on homicide, and his own laws were written on wooden boards called axones, displayed for the public. The name of the harsh lawgiver lives on as an adjective; the laws themselves didn’t last.

cards.headline: Wealth, not birth
cards.body: Solon also sorted citizens into four classes by income, measured in farm produce; the top class harvested at least 500 measures a year. Higher classes could hold higher offices, and even the poorest, the thetes, kept their place in the Assembly. Political privilege now depended on wealth, not noble birth. Not democracy yet, but a rich farmer no longer needed a famous grandfather.

cards.headline: Then he left town
cards.body: Then Solon did something rare for a man with power: he left. He set off on a journey, saying he wouldn’t be back for ten years, rather than be pressed to change his laws. Imagine writing the house rules and then leaving the country so nobody can talk you into rewriting them.

title: Cleisthenes and Democracy
objective: After this level you can explain how Cleisthenes created democracy in 508 BCE.
summary: After the tyrants fell, Cleisthenes (508-507 BCE) mixed Attica into ten new tribes and a Council of 500 chosen by lot: the start of demokratia.

cards.headline: In 508 BCE, one Athenian reshuffled every citizen in Attica.
cards.body: It sounds like paperwork. It’s the moment Athenian democracy began. First, how Athens got there.

cards.headline: From tyrants to a showdown
cards.body: After Solon, Athens fell under tyrants: Peisistratus, then his son Hippias. In 510 BCE the Spartan king Cleomenes marched in and expelled Hippias. Then two nobles fought for control. Isagoras, backed by Sparta, won the top office in 508, but his rival Cleisthenes had the people on his side. When Cleomenes came back to support Isagoras, the Athenians forced them both out.

cards.headline: Shuffle the deck
cards.body: Cleisthenes replaced Athens’ four old tribes, based on descent, with ten new ones. He split Attica into three zones (the city, the coast and the inland) and gave every tribe townships, called demes, from all three. Your rights now came from your deme, which kept its own list of citizens. Like sorting a school into teams that each mix every class, it made tribes less likely to follow local and family loyalties.

mascot.line: Hold on to the lottery. Level 30 asks why Athens counted it more democratic than a vote.

cards.headline: People power, by lottery
cards.body: Each tribe sent 50 men to a new Council of 500. Councillors had to be at least 30 and were chosen by lot every year, and the Council prepared the proposals the Assembly voted on. title: The Assembly
objective: After this level you can explain how Athenian citizens debated and voted.
summary: The Assembly of male citizens met on the Pnyx about 40 times a year, heard any citizen who wished to speak and voted by show of hands.

cards.headline: In Athens you didn’t elect a lawmaker. You were one.
cards.body: If you were a male citizen aged 18 or over, that is. Here’s how the Assembly worked, from the hilltop to the show of hands.

cards.headline: A hill full of voters
cards.body: The Assembly, the ekklesia, was open to every male citizen aged 18 or over. It met in the open on the Pnyx, a rocky hill in Athens with room for about 6,000 people. In the 4th century BCE it met four times in every tenth of the year: 40 meetings a year. It had final control over policy, and it usually voted by a show of hands, with a simple majority deciding.

cards.headline: “Who wishes to speak?”
cards.body: Debate opened with a herald’s invitation, repeated again and again: “Who wishes to address the assembly?” Any citizen could answer it, even a man who earned his living at a trade. The Council of 500 prepared the proposals, but the final say belonged to the crowd on the hill. Picture a town meeting where the carpenter can outtalk the aristocrat.

cards.headline: A red rope, then a paycheck
cards.body: Turnout was a real problem. Aristophanes’ comedy the Acharnians opens with the Pnyx empty while citizens gossip in the marketplace, dodging a rope smeared with red dye. In the early 4th century BCE, Athens tried a carrot instead of a rope: because too few citizens came, it began paying them to attend. Even the first democracy had to get people off the couch.

title: Ostracism
objective: After this level you can explain how Athenians voted to send a citizen away.
summary: In an ostracism, citizens wrote names on potsherds; with enough votes, the man named most left Attica for 10 years, keeping his property.

cards.headline: Once a year, Athens could vote a man out of town.
cards.body: It was an election in reverse, and the ballots were bits of broken pottery.

cards.headline: An election in reverse
cards.body: Each midwinter, the Athenians voted, without debate, on whether to hold an ostracism a few weeks later. If they said yes, each citizen scratched a name on an ostrakon, a piece of broken pottery. If enough votes were cast (6,000, in Plutarch’s account), the man named most had to leave Attica within 10 days and stay away 10 years.

cards.headline: A safety valve
cards.body: Oddly gentle: the exile kept his property. Ostracism, credited to Cleisthenes, aimed at a leading citizen who might threaten the state, and Athens remembered how Peisistratus had made himself tyrant. It was first used in 488-487 BCE and faded out after an ineffective vote, probably in 417. Think of it as removing a player before he can take over the game.

cards.headline: Tired of “the Just”
cards.body: Plutarch tells a story about Aristides, nicknamed “the just.” An illiterate voter, not recognizing him, handed him a sherd and asked him to write “Aristides” on it. Had Aristides ever wronged him? “None at all,” said the man, “neither know I the man; but I am tired of hearing him everywhere called the just.” Aristides wrote his own name.

cards.headline: A well full of Themistocles
cards.body: Real ballots survive. A well on the north slope of the Acropolis held 190 ostraka naming Themistocles, written by just fourteen hands. They seem to have been prepared in advance, ready to hand out. Election-day leaflets, ancient style.

title: Juries and Courts
objective: After this level you can explain how huge citizen juries decided cases.
summary: Athenian juries of hundreds, chosen by lot from 6,000 citizens over 30, heard timed speeches and voted with secret bronze ballots, with no judge.

cards.headline: Imagine a jury of about 500 people, and no judge.
cards.body: In Athens that was ordinary. Big juries, the thinking went, were hard to frighten or buy.

cards.headline: Six thousand jurors a year
cards.body: Each year 6,000 volunteers, male citizens at least 30 years old, were chosen by lot to serve as jurors. A court had about 500 jurors for public cases and about 200 for private ones. There was no judge: jurors decided both the law and the facts, and voted without discussing the case among themselves. Pericles introduced pay for jury service, and critics grumbled that it filled the courts with common people.

cards.headline: Speak for yourself, against the clock
cards.body: There were no lawyers as we know them. Litigants usually spoke for themselves, though others could speak for a defendant. A water clock, the klepsydra, timed each speech: water ran from one pot into another, and when it ran out, so did your turn. It was even stopped while laws and documents were read aloud. No filibusters in Athens.

cards.headline: A secret vote in your fist
cards.body: Each juror got two bronze ballots: one pierced, for the prosecutor, and one solid, for the defendant. They looked identical apart from the axle, so with your fingers over the ends, nobody could see which one you cast. A tie meant the defendant won. The whole system had one goal: large juries made intimidation and bribery harder.

title: Pericles
objective: After this level you can explain Pericles' leadership of Athens' golden age.
summary: Pericles led Athens by winning election as general year after year; Thucydides called it a democracy in name but rule by its leading man.

cards.headline: A democracy with a favorite: Athens kept electing the same man.
cards.body: His name was Pericles. How does one citizen come to lead a city that governs itself?

mascot.line: People mix this up: most officials were drawn by lot, but generals like Pericles were elected.

cards.headline: Elected, not drawn
cards.body: Most Athenian officials were picked by lot, but the ten generals (strategoi) were elected by vote. That was Pericles’ office. Born about 495 BCE, he rose to lead Athens, and after his chief rival was ostracized, Plutarch says, he was re-elected general every year for fifteen years. His power rested on that constant re-election and, as Thucydides saw it, on his intelligence and incorruptibility.

cards.headline: Democracy in name?
cards.body: In Pericles’ funeral speech, as Thucydides records it, Athens’ constitution “favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy.” Yet Thucydides also judged that under Pericles, Athens was a democracy in name but in fact government by its leading man. Both were true at once: the people voted, and they kept voting for him.

cards.headline: Why the helmet?
cards.body: Look at a bust of Pericles and he’s wearing a helmet. Plutarch says his head was long and out of proportion, so almost all his portraits covered it, and comic poets called him “squill-head” (a squill is a sea onion). The most powerful man in Athens still got roasted on stage.

title: The Parthenon
objective: After this level you can describe how and why the Parthenon was built.
summary: After the Persian sack, Pericles rebuilt the Acropolis; the Parthenon (447-438 BCE) honored Athena, held her gold and ivory statue and a league treasury, and was wrecked in 1687.

cards.headline: The Parthenon rose from the ashes of a sack.
cards.body: Enemy troops had wrecked the Acropolis. Athens answered with the most famous temple in Greece, and a fight about who paid for it.

cards.headline: Rebuilding the high city
cards.body: After the Acropolis was sacked during the wars with Persia, Pericles directed a magnificent rebuilding program. Work on the Parthenon began in 447 BCE; the temple was finished by 438, and its outside decoration went on until 432. Its pediments told Athena’s own stories: her birth, and her contest with Poseidon. Remember Level 21’s olive tree? It went up on the temple.

cards.headline: Whose money?
cards.body: The Parthenon also held the treasury of the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states led by Athens. Plutarch reports that Pericles’ enemies accused him of taking the Greeks’ common treasure from the island of Delos and spending it to gild and adorn Athens. It’s the oldest argument in public building: gorgeous, but who paid?

cards.headline: A temple with many lives
cards.body: Inside stood a great gold and ivory statue of Athena by the sculptor Phidias, dedicated in 438 BCE and now lost. The temple itself lived on as a Byzantine church, a Roman Catholic cathedral and then a mosque. In 1687, during fighting between Venice and the Ottomans, gunpowder stored inside exploded and destroyed the center of the building. Using a temple as a powder store: not its best career move.

title: Who Was Left Out
objective: After this level you can explain why women, slaves and foreigners could not vote.
summary: Athenian democracy was for adult male citizens only; citizen women, metics (free foreigners) and enslaved people had no vote.

cards.headline: Athens called itself rule by the people. Which people?
cards.body: Only adult male citizens voted. Women, resident foreigners and enslaved people were left out, and each group was left out for a different reason.

mascot.line: Three groups left out, for three different reasons. Keep them apart and this level is yours.

cards.headline: Citizens, but not voters
cards.body: Athenian women could be citizens, and after 451 or 450 BCE that mattered more than ever: a law carried by Pericles limited citizenship to people with Athenian parents on both sides. Yet only men could vote in the Assembly. In Pericles’ funeral speech, as Thucydides gives it, widows are told that the greatest glory is to be least talked of among men.

cards.headline: Neighbors with no vote
cards.body: Metics were free foreigners living in Athens, including freed slaves, and they made up a large part of the city. They paid a special yearly tax, could not acquire land or a house, and had no direct part in politics. You could live in Athens, work there and pay its taxes, and still be a guest.

cards.headline: Owned, not represented
cards.body: Enslaved people had no voice at all. Athens practiced chattel slavery: people were owned as property, mostly foreigners captured in war or sold by slave traders, and children born to enslaved parents were enslaved too. Rule by the people was never meant to include them.

title: Sparta
objective: After this level you can describe Sparta's unusual society.
summary: Sparta conquered Messenia and made its people helots, state-owned serfs whose labor let every Spartan citizen train for war; two kings ruled at once, and most of what we know comes from outsiders.

cards.headline: Sparta’s citizens didn’t farm, trade or build. Their job was war.
cards.body: Somebody still had to grow the food. The answer explains almost everything strange about Sparta.

cards.headline: Farmland next door
cards.body: Sparta lay in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese, on the Eurotas river. Around 735–715 BCE it conquered its neighbor Messenia, gaining a large tract of fertile land and turning its people into helots. Remember Level 9’s colonists, leaving home short of farmland? Sparta found its farmland next door, and kept the farmers.

cards.headline: The helots
cards.body: Helots were serfs owned by the Spartan state, not by one master. They worked the land and handed over half of their produce, which left Spartan men free to train for war full-time. But helots greatly outnumbered Spartans, by some estimates about seven to one, and Spartans feared a revolt. Each year, officials called ephors formally declared war on the helots, so killing one carried no religious guilt. Sparta’s army wasn’t only for enemies abroad.

cards.headline: Two kings, and a vote by volume
cards.body: Sparta had two hereditary kings at the same time, from two separate royal families. Five ephors served one-year terms, a council of elders led the citizens’ assembly, and the assembly voted by shouting. Picture a company with two bosses, a board that changes every year, and decisions made by whoever cheers loudest.

mascot.line: Ask of every Spartan story: who wrote it, and when? Usually an outsider, often much later.

cards.fact: Most of what we know about Sparta was written by outsiders.
cards.context: Spartans wrote little about themselves. Our accounts come from non-Spartans such as Herodotus, Xenophon and Plutarch, and Plutarch lived from about 46 CE, centuries after Sparta’s great days. So this chapter keeps asking of each Spartan story: evidence, or legend?

title: Growing Up Spartan
objective: After this level you can describe the harsh training of Spartan boys.
summary: At seven, Spartan boys left home for the agoge: barracks life to about thirty, short rations, stealing encouraged. A pit near Taygetus held no newborns.

cards.headline: At seven, a Spartan boy left home. The state raised him from then on.
cards.body: Some of what we’re told about Spartan childhood is well attested. Some of it, the bones have now tested.

cards.headline: Raised by the state
cards.body: From the age of seven, Spartan boys entered the agoge, the state’s training system. They lived in barracks, grouped by age, away from their families, and the training and barracks life lasted until a man was about 30. Picture boarding school, boot camp and a sports academy rolled into one, with no weekends home.

cards.headline: Hungry on purpose
cards.body: Boys in the agoge got little food and were encouraged to steal more. The Greek writer Xenophon says a boy caught stealing was beaten, not for the theft but for doing it badly: getting caught was the failure. The lesson was cunning. Few schools have made “don’t get caught” part of the curriculum.

mascot.line: This is Level 31’s warning at work: a story told centuries later, tested against bones.

cards.fact: Plutarch said Sparta threw away weak babies. The bones disagree.
cards.context: Plutarch wrote that elders inspected every newborn and had weak ones left at a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus. But in 2007 an anthropologist who studied bones from a pit near Mount Taygetus found adolescents and adults aged 18 to 35, and no newborns. A story told centuries later met the evidence, and lost.

summary: Spartan girls trained in athletics and Spartan women could inherit and own land and ran estates, unusual freedoms in Greece; they still had no vote, office or place in the assembly.

cards.headline: “Come back with your shield, or on it.”
cards.body: Later Greek writers put those words in the mouth of a Spartan mother sending her son to war. Legend or not, Spartan women had a reputation no other Greek women had.

cards.headline: Girls in training
cards.body: Spartan girls exercised like the boys: running, wrestling, throwing the discus and javelin. They weren’t trained for battle. Xenophon gives the reason: strong parents, Spartans believed, would have stronger children. So the freedom had a purpose, and the purpose was the army.

cards.headline: Owners and managers
cards.body: Spartan women could inherit and own land. And with the men so often away, they ran homes, farms and estates. Aristotle wrote that nearly two-fifths of Sparta’s land was owned by women, and he listed it among Sparta’s faults. He meant it as a complaint. Today it reads as one of the most surprising facts about the ancient Greek world.

cards.headline: Where the freedom stopped
cards.body: Spartan women still could not vote, hold public office or attend the citizens’ assembly. Freer than most Greek women, yes. Equal to Spartan men, no.

title: The Persian Empire
objective: After this level you can describe the empire that invaded Greece.
summary: Persia’s Achaemenid Empire, begun by Cyrus around 550 BCE, ran from Egypt to the Indus with a Royal Road of relay couriers; when Athens helped the Ionian Revolt, Darius vowed revenge.

cards.headline: Every dinner, a servant told Persia’s king: “Master, remember the Athenians.”
cards.body: Herodotus says Darius ordered it. Why would the ruler of the largest empire the world had yet known brood over one Greek city?

cards.headline: The biggest empire yet
cards.body: Persia’s Achaemenid Empire began with the conquests of Cyrus the Great around 550 BCE. At its height it stretched from Egypt to the Indus River and westward into parts of Greece: the largest empire the world had yet known. It was divided into provinces called satrapies, each owing a fixed yearly tribute. Next to that, a Greek city-state was a dot on the map.

cards.headline: News at relay speed
cards.body: Darius I built the Royal Road, running more than 2,400 km (1,500 miles) from Susa, the Persian capital, to Sardis near the Aegean coast. Ordinary travelers took about three months. Royal messengers, handing off at relay stations, did it in nine days. Herodotus wrote that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stopped them.

cards.fact: Herodotus’s line about Persian couriers is carved on a New York post office.
cards.context: An adapted version runs across the James A. Farley Post Office. Many people take it for the US Postal Service’s motto, but the Postal Service has no official motto. America’s most famous mail slogan was first written about Persia’s royal messengers.

cards.headline: The spark
cards.body: The Greek cities of Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey, lived under Persian rule. In 499 BCE they revolted. Athens sent help, and Sardis was burned. The revolt was crushed by 494 BCE, but Darius used Athens’s part in it as his reason to invade Greece in 490 BCE. Hence the dinner reminder.

title: Marathon
objective: After this level you can explain the Battle of Marathon and the legend of the runner.
summary: In 490 BCE about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans beat a larger Persian force at Marathon with strong wings; Pheidippides ran to Sparta, and the run to Athens is later legend.

cards.headline: Marathon is famous for a run. The real runner went the other way.
cards.body: In 490 BCE Athens faced Persia’s army almost alone. Here’s how it won, and what really happened to the runner.

cards.headline: Almost alone
cards.body: In September 490 BCE a Persian force landed on the plain of Marathon, about 40 km (25 miles) from Athens. Athens asked Sparta for help, but the Spartans said they could not march until the full moon. So about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 men from little Plataea faced a larger Persian force by themselves.

cards.headline: Strong wings, thin middle
cards.body: The Athenian general Miltiades strengthened the two ends of his line and left the center thin. The Persians pushed back the center, and the Greek wings turned inward and surrounded them. Herodotus counted 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenians. Even if his count is generous, it was a rout.

cards.headline: Which run?
cards.body: Herodotus does record a runner: Pheidippides, sent from Athens to Sparta before the battle to ask for help, covering about 240 km (150 miles) in about two days. The famous dash from Marathon to Athens to announce victory isn’t in Herodotus; it’s a later legend. The modern marathon race honors the legend, not the longer run that happened.

cards.fact: The Spartans did come. After it was over.
cards.context: Herodotus says 2,000 Spartans reached Attica on the third day after leaving Sparta, too late for the battle. They went to see the Persian dead at Marathon, praised the Athenians and went home.

title: Thermopylae
objective: After this level you can explain the stand of the 300 Spartans.
summary: In 480 BCE about 7,000 Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas held Thermopylae for two days; after a local showed Persia a path, far more than 300 made the last stand.

cards.headline: “The 300” were never alone at Thermopylae.
cards.body: Legend remembers 300 Spartans. The real stand, in 480 BCE, had thousands of Greeks, a traitor and a mountain path.

cards.headline: A gate between mountain and sea
cards.body: In 480 BCE Xerxes, son of Darius, invaded Greece by land. Herodotus claimed he had more than 2.6 million fighting men; modern estimates run from about 70,000 to 300,000. Either way, the Greeks needed a place where a small force could block a large army. At Thermopylae the road squeezed into a line only a few dozen yards wide, between a steep hillside and the sea.

cards.headline: Two days, then a path
cards.body: Leonidas, a Spartan king, led about 7,000 Greeks, including 300 Spartans, and they held the pass for two days. Then a local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around it. A wall of shields is only as good as its flanks.

mascot.line: “The 300” is the title. Remember the full cast: helots and Boeotians stayed too.

cards.headline: Who stayed
cards.body: Leonidas sent most of the army away. Staying with him were his 300, some helots, and about 1,100 Boeotians from Thespiae and Thebes. They held one more day, and many, if not all, were killed. “The 300” makes a great title. It just leaves out more than a thousand people.

cards.fact: Told the Persian arrows would hide the sun, a Spartan said: then we’ll fight in the shade.
cards.context: Herodotus gives the line to a Spartan named Dieneces. Plutarch, writing centuries later, gave it to Leonidas. Good lines have a way of drifting toward famous people.

title: Salamis
objective: After this level you can explain how the Greek fleet won at Salamis.
summary: Themistocles turned silver into 200 triremes; in 480 BCE, with Athens sacked, he lured Persia’s larger fleet into the strait of Salamis. Plataea ended the invasion.

cards.headline: In 480 BCE the Athenians abandoned their city. Then they won at sea.
cards.body: It started with a lucky strike in a silver mine and a man who didn’t want to share it out.

cards.headline: Silver into ships
cards.body: When Athens’s state-owned silver mines struck a rich vein, Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to spend the windfall on the navy. By 480 BCE Athens had 200 triremes: warships rowed by about 170 men in three tiers, with a bronze-covered ram at the bow. Think of a trireme as a torpedo powered by people.

cards.headline: A city made of ships
cards.body: After Thermopylae, Greece lay open. Athenians sent their women and children to the Peloponnese, and much of the population sheltered on the island of Salamis. The Persians sacked Athens itself. For a while, the city of Athens was its fleet.

cards.headline: The trap in the strait
cards.body: Themistocles sent Xerxes a false message, and the much larger Persian fleet attacked into the narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland. Packed together, its ships could hardly maneuver, and the Greek triremes rammed them. The Greeks sank about 300 Persian ships and lost about 40. Numbers help less when there’s no room to use them.

cards.fact: Xerxes watched it all from the shore.
cards.context: Herodotus says he sat at the foot of a hill facing Salamis, with scribes noting who fought well. Afterward he went home to Susa, and in 479 BCE a Greek victory on land at Plataea ended the invasion.

title: The Delian League
objective: After this level you can explain how Athens turned an alliance into an empire.
summary: Founded in 478 BCE against Persia, the Delian League paid for a fleet Athens led; Athens stopped members leaving and took the treasury, making the league an empire.

cards.headline: Athens’s allies paid for its navy. Then they found they couldn’t leave.
cards.body: An alliance against Persia slowly became an Athenian empire. Here’s how a club turned into a cage.

cards.headline: A league with an island bank
cards.body: In 478 BCE, with Persia beaten back but not gone, Athens and many Greek cities formed an alliance to protect themselves from Persia. Its treasury sat in the temple of Apollo on the island of Delos, which is why we call it the Delian League. Athens supplied the commanders and decided which members gave ships and which gave money.

cards.headline: Money in, ships out
cards.body: Over time most members paid money instead of sending ships, and the tribute built and maintained the fleet Athens led. Around 330 cities appear in the surviving tribute lists. Remember Level 37’s triremes? Now the allies were paying for them, while their own navies faded.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: an alliance against Persia became an empire its members couldn’t leave.

cards.headline: No exit
cards.body: When Naxos tried to leave, Athens attacked and forced it back in. In 454 BCE Athens moved the treasury from Delos to Athens, and the league became, in effect, an Athenian empire. League money even helped pay for Pericles’ rebuilding of Athens, including the Parthenon. The allies had joined a club. Now they were paying rent.

title: The Peloponnesian War
objective: After this level you can explain why Athens and Sparta fought for 27 years.
summary: From 431 to 404 BCE Athens’s navy fought Sparta’s army; Thucydides blamed Spartan fear of Athens. Plague hit Athens, and Sparta, with Persian aid, won.

cards.headline: The Greeks who beat Persia together fought each other for 27 years.
cards.body: And at the end, Persia helped decide who won.

cards.headline: Sea power against land power
cards.body: From 431 to 404 BCE Athens, leading the Delian League, fought Sparta, leading the Peloponnesian League. Athens had the stronger navy; Sparta’s alliance had the stronger army on land. Thucydides, who lived through the war and wrote its history, said the real cause was Athens’s growing power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

cards.headline: Safe behind the walls
cards.body: Under Pericles, Athens avoided Sparta’s army, kept its people inside the city walls and relied on its navy. Then, in 430 BCE, plague struck the crowded city. It killed tens of thousands, including Pericles. Thucydides caught it too, and survived to write about it. The plan to stay safe had packed everyone together for the disease.

cards.headline: Persian gold, Spartan ships
cards.body: Athens lost a huge expedition to Sicily in 415–413 BCE. Then, in 405 BCE, the Spartan admiral Lysander, with much aid from Persia, destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami. Athens surrendered in 404 BCE. Persia had lost to the Greeks at Salamis. In the end, it helped sink Athens anyway.

cards.fact: Athens’s walls came down to flute music.
cards.context: Xenophon says the victors tore them down to the music of flute girls, thinking that day the beginning of freedom for Greece. The Delian League was disbanded the same year.

title: The Twelve Olympians
objective: After this level you can name the main Greek gods and what each ruled.
summary: The Greeks said their twelve great gods lived on Mount Olympus, Greece’s highest peak; the lists of the twelve varied, and the gods looked and acted like people.

cards.headline: The Greek gods had a real address: the highest mountain in Greece.
cards.body: Who was said to live up there, what did each one rule, and who got a seat at the table?

cards.headline: A home on the highest peak
cards.body: Remember Level 2? Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece. The Greeks gave their gods the tallest one. Mount Olympus rises 2,917 m (9,570 feet), the highest peak in Greece, and they regarded it as the home of the gods and the site of Zeus’s throne. That’s why the great gods are called the Olympians. In a land full of mountains, the gods took the penthouse.

items.label: Craftsman and courier

cards.headline: The twelfth seat
cards.body: Ask the Greeks to name all twelve and you’d get more than one answer. One common list runs Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and Dionysus. Other lists seat Hestia, goddess of the hearth, or even Hades instead. Twelve chairs, and the guest list kept changing.

mascot.line: Hold on to these very human gods. Level 51’s philosophers pick a fight with them.

cards.headline: Gods who acted like people
cards.body: What made these gods feel so Greek? Greek religion pictured many gods in human form, with one supreme god over them. They looked like people, and they behaved like people too. In Greek stories Hera, queen of the gods, keeps appearing as Zeus’s jealous, vengeful wife, hounding the women he loved. Gods, yes, but with very human tempers.

title: Zeus
objective: After this level you can describe Zeus, king of the gods, and his thunderbolt.
summary: In myth Zeus was hidden on Crete from Cronus, who swallowed his children, then overthrew the Titans, got his thunderbolt from the Cyclopes and drew the sky when the brothers split the world.

cards.headline: Zeus survived babyhood because his mother fed his father a rock.
cards.body: It’s one of the strangest family stories ever told, and the Greeks told it about their king of the gods, ruler of the sky.

cards.headline: A father who swallowed his children
cards.body: The Greeks told it like this. Cronus, king of the Titans, learned that one of his children was fated to overthrow him. His solution was brutal: each time his wife, Rhea, gave birth, he swallowed the baby. One child after another disappeared down his throat. Family dinners in that house were tense.

cards.headline: The stone in swaddling clothes
cards.body: When Zeus was born, Rhea made a swap. She hid the baby in a cave on Crete and handed Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, and he swallowed it. Yes, Crete: the island of Level 3’s Minoans. Zeus grew up, forced Cronus to cough up his brothers and sisters, and with his brothers Hades and Poseidon beat Cronus and the Titans.

cards.headline: Thunder, made to order
cards.body: Where did the famous thunderbolt come from? The poet Hesiod said the Cyclopes forged it: three craftsmen named Thunder, Lightning and Bright Flash. They made Poseidon’s trident and a helmet of invisibility for Hades too. Remember Level 4’s Cyclopean walls? Same giants. Zeus became the sky and weather god, sender of thunder, lightning, rain and winds.

cards.headline: Splitting the world
cards.body: After the victory, the three brothers divided the world, and they did it by drawing lots. Zeus got the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld. The biggest inheritance in Greek myth was settled the way you’d decide who does the dishes.

title: Poseidon
objective: After this level you can describe Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes.
summary: Poseidon drew the sea by lot; with his trident he also ruled earthquakes and horses, and myths said he punished Argos after losing it to Hera.

cards.headline: The Greek god of the sea was also the god of earthquakes.
cards.body: Sea, shaking ground and horses: an odd set of jobs for one god. Meet Poseidon.

cards.headline: Lord of the sea
cards.body: Remember Level 42’s lottery? When Zeus and his brothers split the world, the sea fell to Poseidon. In a land where the sea opened up wider horizons (Level 2), that was a big realm. His weapon and main symbol was the trident, perhaps once a fish spear. The Romans later matched him with their own sea god, Neptune. The mightiest weapon in the sea may have started as fishing gear.

cards.headline: The earth-shaker
cards.body: Poseidon ruled more than water. He was the god of earthquakes, and Greeks called him enosichthōn, “earth-shaker”. He was the god of horses as well; in some myths he created the horse. The same god who stirred the waves could rattle the ground under your feet. Wherever things heaved, rolled or galloped, Poseidon was in charge.

mascot.line: Sound familiar? In Level 21 he lost Athens to Athena, too.

cards.headline: A sore loser
cards.body: Poseidon wanted cities, too. He contested Argos with Hera, and lost. In one version he flooded the land in revenge. In the version the ancient writer Pausanias tells, he made the rivers of Argos disappear, which is why, Pausanias says, they give no water except after rain. A myth that doubles as a weather report.

title: Athena and Apollo
objective: After this level you can describe Athena and Apollo and what they stood for.
summary: Athena, born armed from Zeus’s head, stood for war with a plan, crafts and practical reason; Apollo, Artemis’s twin, carried the bow and the lyre and was god of prophecy and healing.

cards.headline: One Greek goddess was born out of her father’s head, fully armed and shouting.
cards.body: That was Athena. Her half-brother Apollo arrived more quietly, carrying a bow in one hand and a lyre in the other. What did each of them stand for?

cards.headline: Born with a battle cry
cards.body: The Greeks said Athena burst from Zeus’s forehead fully grown, in armor, and giving a battle cry. One version explains how she got in there: Zeus had swallowed her pregnant mother, Metis, goddess of counsel. Remember Cronus in Level 42, swallowing his children? Swallowing relatives seems to run in the family.

cards.headline: War with a plan
cards.body: Athena was a goddess of war, handicraft and practical reason. Her kind of war was the thinking kind: strategy, not the violence and bloodlust of Ares. She was patroness of spinning and weaving too, and her owl became famous as the symbol of Athens. Ares brought the fury; Athena brought the plan.

cards.headline: The bow and the lyre
cards.body: Apollo and his twin sister, Artemis, were born on the island of Delos, children of Zeus and Leto. Apollo carried two symbols. His bow stood for distance, death, terror and awe; his lyre stood for joy through music, poetry and dance. He was a god of prophecy and healing as well. The same god could strike you from afar or play you a song.

cards.headline: The bright one
cards.body: Apollo had another name, Phoebus, meaning “bright” or “pure”, and in time he came to be connected with the Sun. So when a poem hails “Phoebus Apollo”, it’s calling him the bright one.

title: The Underworld
objective: After this level you can describe Hades and the Greek underworld.
summary: Hades ruled the underworld that shared his name; Charon ferried the buried dead for a coin, Cerberus guarded the way, and Persephone’s months below explained winter.

cards.headline: In Greek myth, even the dead had to pay their fare.
cards.body: A ferryman, a guard dog and a god who shared his name with his kingdom. Welcome to the underworld.

cards.headline: One name, two meanings
cards.body: Hades was the god of the underworld, and his realm, the house of Hades, came to share his name. It fell to him by lot, remember, when Zeus drew the sky and Poseidon the sea. He was also called Pluto, “Wealth”, perhaps because he gathered every living thing into his treasury at death. Sooner or later, everyone ends up at his place.

cards.headline: The ferry fare
cards.body: To get in, a soul had to cross the water. Charon ferried the dead over the rivers Styx and Acheron, but only those who had received the rites of burial. His fare was the coin placed in the corpse’s mouth. No funeral, no ferry.

cards.headline: The dog at the door
cards.body: Waiting on the far side was Cerberus, the monstrous watchdog of the underworld. He usually had three heads, though the poet Hesiod gave him 50, and snakes grew from his back. His job worked in both directions: keep the living out, and devour any of the dead who tried to escape. The underworld had a one-way door.

mascot.line: Keep this one: a myth doing a job. Persephone’s months below explain winter.

cards.headline: Why winter comes
cards.body: Hades’ queen was Persephone, daughter of Demeter, Level 41’s grain goddess. The Greeks told how Hades carried her off while she was gathering flowers. Because she ate a pomegranate seed below, she had to spend a third of every year with him (more, in some versions). While she was gone, Demeter grieved and the fields lay barren. A myth that turns the seasons into a family story.

title: Heracles
objective: After this level you can describe the Twelve Labors of Heracles.
summary: Hounded by Hera, Heracles served Eurystheus at Tiryns to win immortality; he was set ten labors, but two were not counted, so they became twelve.

cards.headline: Heracles was set ten impossible jobs. His boss refused to count two of them.
cards.body: That’s how the Ten Labors became the famous Twelve. But why was a son of Zeus taking orders at all?

cards.headline: Hated from the cradle
cards.body: Heracles was the son of Zeus and a mortal woman, Alcmene, and Zeus’s wife, Hera, persecuted him for it. She sent two serpents to kill him in his cradle; the baby strangled them. Remember Level 41’s jealous Hera? This is her at full strength.

cards.headline: Why the labors
cards.body: Hera struck again when he was grown. She drove him mad, and he killed his wife, Megara, and their children. Afterwards he asked the oracle at Delphi where he should live. The answer: in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and performing ten labors; then he would become immortal. Tiryns? One of Level 4’s Mycenaean strongholds.

cards.fact: Heracles’ first labor was killing the Nemean lion. He wore its skin ever after.
cards.context: Then came the nine-headed Hydra of Lerna, a wild boar, man-eating birds and more. The last labor took him down to the underworld to fetch up Cerberus, Level 45’s three-headed watchdog. Of all the dogs in myth, that’s the one you’d least want to walk.

cards.headline: Ten became twelve
cards.body: So why twelve? Eurystheus refused to count two. The Hydra didn’t count, he said, because Heracles’ companion Iolaus had helped. The Augean stables didn’t count either, because Heracles, who cleaned them in a single day by diverting two rivers, did the job for hire. Even myth has fine print. In the end, the Greeks said, his divine part rose to heaven and he became a god.

title: Perseus and Medusa
objective: After this level you can retell Perseus's quest.
summary: Cast adrift because of a prophecy, Perseus beheaded Medusa by watching her reflection, killed his grandfather by accident and was said to have founded Mycenae.

cards.headline: A prophecy said a baby would kill his grandfather. So Grandpa set him adrift.
cards.body: The baby was Perseus. The sea didn’t stop the prophecy; it only postponed it.

cards.headline: Cast adrift
cards.body: Acrisius of Argos had been told his grandson would kill him. So when his daughter, Danaë, had a son, Perseus, he shut mother and baby in a chest and cast it into the sea. The chest grounded on the island of Seriphus, and Perseus grew up there. Problem postponed, not solved.

cards.headline: An impossible errand
cards.body: On Seriphus, King Polydectes wanted Danaë, and he tricked Perseus into promising to bring him the head of Medusa. Medusa was the most famous of the monsters called Gorgons, and the only one who could die. Her hair was snakes, and anyone who looked at her face turned instantly to stone. Some errand.

cards.headline: Don’t look
cards.body: Perseus went well equipped: winged sandals, the cap of Hades that made him invisible, and a curved sword. The real trick came from Athena, a shield: he guided himself by Medusa’s reflection and never met her eyes. From her neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, and her head ended up on Athena’s aegis. cards.headline: The prophecy comes true
cards.body: Back on Seriphus, Perseus turned Polydectes and his supporters to stone. Later, throwing the discus, he accidentally struck and killed Acrisius. The prophecy came true after all. Perseus was also said to have founded Mycenae, Level 4’s stronghold, and Pausanias heard the name came from a mykes: the cap of his scabbard that fell there, or a mushroom.

title: Theseus and the Minotaur
objective: After this level you can retell the myth of the Labyrinth.
summary: Theseus ended Minos’s tribute of young Athenians by killing the Minotaur, finding his way out with Ariadne’s thread, the clew that gave us the word clue.

cards.headline: Every time you look for a clue, you’re following a Greek myth.
cards.body: The word began as a ball of thread in the Labyrinth on Crete. Here’s how it got there.

mascot.line: This is Level 3’s myth again: the King Minos that Evans named the Minoans after.

cards.headline: A terrible tribute
cards.body: Remember Level 3’s myth: King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus. To avenge his son Androgeos, killed by Athenians, Minos made Athens send seven youths and seven maidens to be devoured by it: every ninth year in one version, every year in another. Fourteen young Athenians, fed to a monster.

cards.headline: Theseus volunteers
cards.body: When the third tribute came due, Theseus volunteered to go. He was the son of King Aegeus of Athens (or, in another version, of Poseidon). On Crete, Minos’s own daughter, Ariadne, helped him: with her thread, he found his way back out of the Labyrinth after killing the Minotaur. The enemy king’s daughter handed the hero the way home.

cards.fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew”, a ball of thread.
cards.context: Its meaning shifted because of the clew Ariadne gave Theseus to guide him out of the Labyrinth. The spelling “clue” appears by the mid-1400s, and by the 1620s a clue could be anything that points the way, maze or no maze. Every detective story owes Ariadne a thank-you note.

cards.headline: The wrong sail
cards.body: Theseus had promised his father a signal: if he survived, his ship would come home under a white sail instead of the usual black one. He forgot. Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and killed himself; in one version he drowned himself in the sea, which was called the Aegean ever after. The hero won, and his father never knew.

title: The Voyage of Odysseus
