summary: Odysseus tricked and blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, earning Poseidon’s anger, heard the Sirens tied to the mast and lost six men passing Scylla and Charybdis.

cards.headline: Odysseus beat a one-eyed giant with a joke about his own name.
cards.body: Level 6 said the Odyssey follows Odysseus’s ten-year struggle to get home. Here are some of the monsters that made it take so long.

cards.headline: My name is Nobody
cards.body: Odysseus and his men were trapped in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus told the giant his name was “Noman”: Nobody. Then he blinded him with a heated olive-wood stake. When Polyphemus shouted to the other Cyclopes that Noman was killing him, they told him to pray to Poseidon and went away. Nobody ever used an alibi so well.

cards.headline: Poseidon’s grudge
cards.body: There was a catch. Polyphemus was Poseidon’s son, and he prayed to his father for revenge. Remember Level 43’s sore loser? Poseidon answered by delaying Odysseus’s homecoming with shipwrecks and other disasters, and Odysseus finally reached home as the only survivor. Blind the sea god’s son, and the sea itself turns against you.

cards.headline: A song to die for
cards.body: Then came the Sirens, part bird and part woman, whose sweet song lured sailors to destruction; Homer has two of them. Odysseus stopped his crew’s ears with wax and had himself tied to the mast, so he couldn’t steer the ship off course. He heard the deadliest song in the world, strapped in like a passenger.

cards.headline: Between Scylla and Charybdis
cards.body: Next, two monsters guarded narrow waters so close together that no ship could pass without meeting one or both. Odysseus steered closer to Scylla, lost six men to her, and got through. The pair was later placed in the Strait of Messina. We still say “between Scylla and Charybdis”: stuck between two equally bad choices.

title: What Is Philosophy?
objective: After this level you can explain what Greek philosophers were trying to do.
summary: Philosophy means love of wisdom. The first Greek philosophers, in 6th-century BCE Ionia, looked for causes in nature, and Xenophanes questioned Homer’s gods.

cards.headline: In the 6th century BCE, some Greeks started asking “why?” and wouldn’t stop.
cards.body: No labs, no telescopes, just arguments. This chapter follows the people who turned asking questions into a way of life. First: what were they after?

cards.headline: Love of wisdom
cards.body: The word philosophy is Greek: philosophia, “love of wisdom”. Philo- is the love part, and sophia is wisdom. Notice what the name doesn’t say. A philosopher isn’t someone who owns wisdom, like a trophy on a shelf. It’s someone who loves it and goes looking for it. You can love something you haven’t caught yet.

mascot.line: Hold on to this: causes inside nature. The rest of this chapter builds on it.

cards.headline: Causes inside nature
cards.body: The first Greek philosophers lived in Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey, in the 6th century BCE. Their big move was to look for causes within nature itself, not in the whims of gods who behaved like people. Thales, who gets Level 52 to himself, is counted as the first. Swap “the gods willed it” for “here’s how it works”, and you’ve got the idea.

cards.headline: Xenophanes picks a fight with Homer
cards.body: Remember Level 6? Homer was the basis of Greek education: Greece’s textbook. In the 500s BCE the thinker Xenophanes attacked it: Homer and Hesiod, he complained, gave the gods theft, adultery and deceit, things people get blamed for. Then his sharpest jab: if horses or oxen had hands and could draw, they’d draw gods that looked like horses and oxen.

cards.fact: Ethiopians say their gods are snub-nosed and black; Thracians say theirs are blue-eyed and red-haired.
cards.context: That’s Xenophanes again, noticing that each people’s gods look like that people. Taking a story everyone grew up with and questioning it out loud, with reasons: that’s philosophy in action.

title: Thales and the First Questions
objective: After this level you can explain how early thinkers looked for natural explanations.
summary: Thales of Miletus said everything comes from water and explained earthquakes without Poseidon; Anaximander and Anaximenes offered the boundless and air.

cards.headline: The first philosopher, the story goes, fell into a well while stargazing.
cards.body: In Plato’s telling, a Thracian servant girl mocked him for gazing at the sky while missing what was at his feet. So what was Thales looking for up there?

cards.headline: Everything is water
cards.body: Thales lived in Miletus, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey, in the early 6th century BCE. According to Aristotle, he said water is the origin of all things, and that the earth rests on water. Why water? Aristotle guessed that Thales noticed the food of every creature is moist, and seeds are moist too. Look around your kitchen: it’s not a crazy guess.

mascot.line: Wrong answer, right kind of answer: a natural cause people could argue about. That’s the key.

cards.headline: Earthquakes without Poseidon
cards.body: Now the bold part. The Roman writer Seneca reports that Thales used his floating earth to explain earthquakes: the land rides on water like a boat, and rough water rocks it. The old answer was an angry god, Poseidon, shaking the ground. Thales was wrong. But he offered a natural cause that people could argue about and improve, and that was new.

cards.headline: Arguing with the teacher
cards.body: Improving is exactly what happened next, in the same city. Anaximander, Thales’s pupil or associate, said the source of everything wasn’t water but the apeiron, “the boundless”. Anaximenes, a third thinker from Miletus, chose air: thin it and it becomes fire; thicken it and it turns to wind, cloud, water, earth and finally stone. One city, three thinkers, three answers.

title: Pythagoras
objective: After this level you can describe Pythagoras and his followers.
summary: Pythagoras led a rule-bound community at Croton in southern Italy; his followers believed souls are reborn in animals and that all things are numbers.

cards.headline: “Stop beating that puppy!” said Pythagoras. “It has a dead friend’s soul.”
cards.body: That story comes from Xenophanes, the critic from Level 51, and he told it as a joke. But a joke needs a real target. What did Pythagoras believe?

cards.headline: Souls that move house
cards.body: Pythagoreans believed that after death a human soul is reborn in other animals, so all living things are kin. That’s what Xenophanes was mocking: a friend’s soul, now in a puppy. The belief came with a whole way of life, run by strict rules. Pythagoreans wore white, entered temples barefoot and, most famously, did not eat beans.

cards.headline: A brotherhood in Italy
cards.body: Pythagoras grew up on the island of Samos and, about 530 BCE, moved to Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy. There he gathered followers into a community. Later tradition says newcomers had to keep silent for five years. Pythagoras seems to have written no books, so what we know of him comes from other, mostly later, writers. Legends grow fast in that kind of silence.

cards.headline: All things are numbers
cards.body: Pythagoreans found numbers hiding in music. The central harmonies, the octave, the fifth and the fourth, match the simple whole-number ratios 2 : 1, 3 : 2 and 4 : 3. If something as moving as music runs on arithmetic, what else might? The Pythagoreans’ answer: everything. Numbers were the key to the world, summed up as “all things are numbers”.

cards.fact: The Pythagorean theorem is older than Pythagoras.
cards.context: Babylonian tablets from about 1900–1600 BCE already show knowledge of it, and there’s no evidence Pythagoras proved it himself. He got his name on it anyway. Some people have all the luck.

title: Socrates
objective: After this level you can explain Socrates' method of questioning.
summary: Socrates wrote nothing and is known through Plato and Xenophon. He questioned people who seemed wise, testing their definitions, and turned philosophy toward how to live.

cards.headline: The oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser than Socrates. He set out to check.
cards.body: In Plato’s telling, his friend Chaerephon asked the question, and the answer puzzled Socrates, who didn’t think he was wise at all. His way of checking changed philosophy.

mascot.line: Insider tip: when you read “Socrates said”, hear “Plato or Xenophon says he said.”

cards.headline: Known only through others
cards.body: First, a warning label. Socrates, who lived in Athens from about 470 to 399 BCE, wrote nothing. We know him mainly through two of his followers, Plato and Xenophon. So whenever you read “Socrates said”, it really means “Plato or Xenophon says Socrates said”. The most famous talker in philosophy never left us a single word of his own.

cards.headline: Testing the oracle
cards.body: Socrates went to people with a reputation for wisdom: politicians, poets, craftsmen. He questioned them and found they thought they knew things they didn’t. His verdict, in Plato’s Apology: he was wiser in only one small way. What he didn’t know, he didn’t think he knew. Knowing what you don’t know turns out to be a head start.

cards.headline: How the questions worked
cards.body: His method, the elenchus, tested definitions until the contradictions showed. In Plato’s Laches, a general defines courage as staying at your post and not running away. But, Socrates asks, can’t a retreat take courage too? Try again: courage is endurance of the soul. Then is foolish endurance courage? The dialogue ends with no answer, and two men who know they don’t know.

cards.headline: Down from the heavens
cards.body: Remember Thales, gazing at the stars and asking what everything is made of? Socrates turned philosophy around. As the Roman writer Cicero put it, Socrates was the first to call philosophy down from the heavens and bring it into cities and homes, to ask about life, morals, good and evil. Not what the world is made of, but how you should live in it.

title: The Trial of Socrates
objective: After this level you can explain why Athens sentenced Socrates to death.
summary: In 399 BCE Socrates was tried for impiety and corrupting the young, amid suspicion over his companion Critias; convicted narrowly, he drank hemlock.

cards.headline: In 399 BCE, Athens put a philosopher of about 70 on trial for his life.
cards.body: His accusers said his questions had done real harm. How does asking questions become a crime?

cards.headline: The charges
cards.body: The charges were impiety, not honoring the city’s gods, and corrupting the young. The accusers were Meletus, Anytus and Lycon, and the case went to a jury of about 500 citizens. In his defense, as Plato tells it, Socrates called himself a gadfly stuck to Athens, a big, sluggish horse that needed stinging awake. Horses tend to swat gadflies.

cards.headline: Why then?
cards.body: Timing mattered. After Athens lost its war with Sparta, a group called the Thirty Tyrants, led by Critias, ruled the city in 404–403 BCE. Critias had been a companion of Socrates. An amnesty in 403 BCE had closed that chapter, and the formal charges were about gods and the young. But suspicion of Critias’s old companion hadn’t gone away.

cards.headline: A cheeky counter-offer
cards.body: Socrates was found guilty; in Plato’s Apology he says that if just 30 votes had gone the other way, he’d have been acquitted. Then he had to propose a penalty. His suggestion: free meals in the Prytaneum, the honor Athens gave Olympic victors. It was not a crowd-pleaser. The jury chose death.

cards.headline: The cup
cards.body: Friends planned to get him out of prison. In Plato’s Crito, Socrates refuses: he must not break Athens’ laws. So he was put to death by drinking hemlock. In Plato’s Phaedo, the numbness rises from his legs until it reaches his heart. Tried for his questions, he chose the laws over escape.

title: Plato
objective: After this level you can describe Plato's Academy and his allegory of the cave.
summary: Plato, Socrates’ student, wrote dialogues and founded the Academy in the 380s BCE. His cave allegory shows prisoners taking shadows for reality.

cards.headline: Imagine you’d spent your whole life watching shadows on a wall.
cards.body: You’d think the shadows were everything. That’s the start of Plato’s most famous story. Before we step into the cave, meet the man who told it.

cards.headline: Socrates’ student
cards.body: Plato, born in Athens around 428 BCE, was a student of Socrates and was deeply affected by his death. He wrote dialogues, usually with Socrates as the main speaker. In the 380s BCE he set up a school outside the walls of Athens, at a grove called the Akademeia: the Academy. Every academy since, including the one on your local school sign, borrows its name.

cards.headline: The cave
cards.body: In the Republic, Plato imagines prisoners chained in a cave, facing a wall. Behind them a fire burns, and the objects moving in front of it cast shadows on the wall. The shadows are all the prisoners have ever seen, so to them, shadows are reality. Now free one prisoner. Dazzled by the fire, he is dragged up into sunlight, where he sees real things, and at last the sun itself.

cards.headline: The way out
cards.body: For Plato, our senses show us shadows: imperfect copies. Real knowledge means climbing toward the Forms, perfect models such as Justice, Beauty and Equality. The sun stands for the highest of all, the Good. Think of every wobbly circle you’ve ever drawn. You still know what a perfect circle is, though you’ve never drawn one.

cards.fact: The prisoners would kill whoever tried to lead them out.
cards.context: The freed man goes back down to tell the others, and they laugh at him. Plato has Socrates say they’d put to death anyone who tried to free them. Many readers hear an echo of Socrates’ own fate. Remember the hemlock in Level 55?

title: Aristotle
objective: After this level you can explain the huge range of things Aristotle studied.
summary: Aristotle studied with Plato for 20 years, then founded the Lyceum. He built the first logic, catalogued over 500 animal species and defined virtue as a mean.

cards.headline: Logic, animals, politics, poetry, ethics: Aristotle wrote about all of them.
cards.body: And that’s the short list. How did one person cover so much? Start with where he learned.

cards.headline: Twenty years with Plato
cards.body: Aristotle was born in 384 BCE in Stagira, in northern Greece. He joined Plato’s Academy in 367 BCE, aged 17, and stayed 20 years as pupil and then colleague. He still argued with his teacher, above all about the Forms. As he put it, friends and truth are both dear, but it’s our duty to prefer the truth. In 335 BCE, back in Athens, he opened his own school: the Lyceum.

cards.headline: A mind without borders
cards.body: His range is dizzying: logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetry. He created the first systematic logic, a theory of correct reasoning. On the island of Lesbos he studied animals, especially sea creatures, and more than 500 species appear in his works. Some of his unlikely-sounding fish stories were proved right many centuries later. Most fish stories go the other way.

cards.headline: Courage, again
cards.body: Remember Level 54, where the Laches ended without defining courage? Aristotle had a go. Each virtue, he argued, is a middle point between too much and too little. The coward flees every danger; the rash person charges at all of them. Courage sits in between: facing the dangers worth facing, with the right amount of fear.

cards.fact: Of perhaps 200 works by Aristotle, about 31 survive.
cards.context: And the survivors read like lecture notes and drafts, not polished books. Next time your notes look messy, take heart: so did Aristotle’s.

title: Stoics and Epicureans
objective: After this level you can compare two Greek schools about how to live well.
summary: Around 300 BCE two schools opened in Athens: Zeno’s Stoics said virtue is the only good; Epicurus said the goal is pleasure, meaning freedom from pain and worry.

cards.headline: Around 300 BCE, two schools opened in Athens: one on a porch, one in a garden.
cards.body: Both asked the same question: how do you live well? Their answers could hardly be more different.

cards.headline: The porch
cards.body: Zeno of Citium came to Athens about 312 BCE and taught in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch; his followers were named Stoics after it. Their core claim: virtue is the only true good. Live in harmony with nature, guided by reason. Strong emotions, they held, are errors of judgment, so reason can correct them. Stuck in traffic? A Stoic would say the traffic isn’t the problem; your judgment about it is.

cards.headline: The garden
cards.body: Epicurus opened his school, the Garden, in Athens around 306 BCE, and it admitted women and enslaved people. He called pleasure the goal of life, but defined it as the absence of pain in the body and trouble in the soul. His school lived mainly on barley bread and water. In one letter he asked for a little pot of cheese, so he could have a feast. Wild times.

title: Diogenes and the Cynics
objective: After this level you can describe Diogenes and why he searched for an honest man.
summary: Diogenes of Sinope, called the Dog, lived in poverty and mocked empty customs. His lamp in daylight searched for a real human being; his pupil Crates taught Zeno.

cards.headline: A man walked through the streets in broad daylight, holding a lit lamp.
cards.body: As he went, he said, “I am looking for a man.” His name was Diogenes, and this was his idea of a lesson.

cards.headline: The Dog
cards.body: Diogenes came from Sinope, a Greek city on the Black Sea coast, and was said to have been exiled for adulterating the coinage. In Athens he lived in poverty, begged for food and slept in public places; later he lived in a large storage jar. He did everything in public, which is probably why people called him the Dog. His followers were the Cynics: in Greek, the dog-like ones.

cards.headline: Looking for a man
cards.body: So what was the lamp for? Diogenes taught that virtue meant living simply, according to nature, and throwing out empty customs and luxury. Tradition remembers his search as one for an “honest man”. But in Diogenes Laertius’s ancient account, he just says he is looking for a man. The jab, it seems: in a city full of people, he couldn’t find one living as a real human being should.

cards.headline: Nobody was safe
cards.body: Stories about him spare no one. When Plato defined a human as a featherless biped, Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it in and said, “Here is Plato’s man.” When Alexander the Great offered him any favor, he replied, “Stand out of my light.” Asked where he came from, he answered: “I am a citizen of the world.”

mascot.line: This connects to Level 58: living by nature runs from the Cynics into the Stoics.

cards.fact: Stoicism has Cynic roots.

title: Euclid's Geometry
objective: After this level you can explain what Euclid’s Elements did for mathematics.
summary: Around 300 BCE in Alexandria, Euclid built the Elements: 13 books proving geometry step by step from a few stated starting points. It set the standard for proof for over 2,000 years.

cards.headline: Around 300 BCE, a Greek wrote a math book. It taught for 2,000 years.
cards.body: Euclid’s Elements didn’t last because it was packed with new facts. It lasted because of how it made you sure of them.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: state your starting points, then prove everything from them.

cards.headline: Start with almost nothing
cards.body: Euclid worked in Alexandria, in Egypt, around 300 BCE. Book I of his Elements opens with 23 definitions (“A point is that which has no part”), then five postulates and five common notions: starting points you accept without proof. Everything after that is proved, step by step, from them alone. Think of a recipe that lists every ingredient up front and never sneaks in a new one halfway through.

cards.headline: Old results, new building
cards.body: Euclid didn’t discover most of it. He compiled the Elements from the work of earlier mathematicians, but the design of the whole was his own. Across 13 books he moves from flat shapes to numbers to solid, three-dimensional figures, and each result rests on the ones proved before it. His real invention was the architecture: a heap of known results turned into one building where every brick holds up the next.

cards.fact: The Elements has had more than 1,000 editions since it was first printed in 1482.
cards.context: Its way of proving things and teaching geometry lasted, practically unchanged, for more than 2,000 years. If you’ve ever written a proof in a geometry class, you’ve worked in Euclid’s style.

cards.headline: No royal road
cards.body: Centuries later, the philosopher Proclus told a story: King Ptolemy asked Euclid for a shorter way to learn geometry than the Elements. Euclid replied that there is no royal road to geometry. True or not, it sums up the book. Every step has to be earned, even if you’re a king.

title: Archimedes
objective: After this level you can explain Archimedes’ discoveries about levers and floating.
summary: Archimedes of Syracuse worked out the law of the lever and showed that an object in a fluid is lighter by the weight of the fluid it displaces. The naked “Eureka!” run is a later embellishment.

cards.headline: Archimedes ran naked through the streets shouting “Eureka!” Probably not.
cards.body: That part is later embellishment. But the science behind the story is real, and so is another idea of his you’ve used on every seesaw.

cards.headline: The seesaw rule
cards.body: Archimedes lived in Syracuse, on Sicily, from about 287 BCE until 212 or 211 BCE. He showed that weights balance on a lever at distances from the pivot in inverse proportion to the weights. That’s the seesaw trick: an adult twice your weight balances you by sitting half as far from the middle. Go far enough out, and a small weight can balance a huge one.

cards.headline: Move the Earth?
cards.body: So a famous line got pinned on him: “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.” It comes from Pappus of Alexandria, writing around 340 CE, more than five centuries later, and it’s probably not Archimedes’ own words. But it is the lever rule, pushed to the limit. With a long enough lever, anything moves. Finding the place to stand is your problem.

mascot.line: Don’t mix the two up: the water test is probably true; the naked “Eureka!” run is embellishment.

cards.headline: Lighter in water
cards.body: In On Floating Bodies, Archimedes showed that a solid denser than a fluid, dipped into it, is lighter by the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. The Roman writer Vitruvius tells how he used water to test whether King Hiero’s gold wreath had been secretly mixed with silver. The test is probably true. The naked dash through the streets shouting “Eureka!” is later embellishment.

title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
objective: After this level you can explain how Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s size.
summary: Eratosthenes compared the noon Sun at Syene and Alexandria, used Euclid’s geometry of parallel lines, and multiplied by 50 to get Earth’s circumference: 250,000 stadia.

cards.headline: His nickname was “Beta”: second best. He measured the whole Earth anyway.
cards.body: No ship, no satellite, no trip around the world. Just a shadow, a rule from geometry and a little multiplication.

cards.headline: Second at everything
cards.body: Eratosthenes was born in Cyrene around 276 BCE, settled in Alexandria and became director of its great library. He worked in so many fields that people called him Beta: like an all-round athlete who takes second prize in every event. A backhanded compliment. But measuring a planet takes astronomy, geography and geometry at once, so a good all-rounder was exactly who you’d want.

mascot.line: This is Level 61’s Euclid at work: a rule about parallel lines, used to measure a planet.

cards.headline: Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: At noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down at Syene, in southern Egypt. At Alexandria it stood about 7° from vertical, about one-fiftieth of a circle. Eratosthenes assumed the Sun’s rays arrive parallel. Then a rule from Level 61’s Euclid does the work: a line crossing two parallel lines makes equal angles with them. So those 7° at Alexandria are also the angle at Earth’s center between the two cities.

cards.headline: Times fifty
cards.body: If the angle is one-fiftieth of a circle, the distance from Syene to Alexandria is one-fiftieth of the way around the world. Multiply it by 50 and you have Earth’s circumference. His answer: 250,000 stadia. How close was that? It depends on how long his stadion was, so estimates of his error run from 0.5 to 17 percent. Not bad for second best.

title: Greek Astronomy
objective: After this level you can explain Greek models of the heavens.
summary: Eudoxus built an Earth-centered sky of 27 nested spheres; Aristarchus put the Sun at the center, an idea no one could test; Hipparchus measured stars and found precession.

cards.headline: The Greeks agreed the heavens moved in circles. They argued about the center.
cards.body: Most put Earth there. One put the Sun there instead. Here’s how Greek astronomers built a sky out of spheres, and why the Sun-centered idea lost.

cards.headline: A sky of nested spheres
cards.body: In the 4th century BCE, Eudoxus of Cnidus modeled the heavens with 27 spheres around Earth: one for the stars, three each for the Sun and Moon, and four for each planet. Picture nesting dolls, all turning around you. His rule that every heavenly motion is uniform and circular stuck: Aristotle endorsed it, and it stayed orthodox until Kepler in the 1600s.

cards.headline: The Sun in the middle
cards.body: Aristarchus of Samos (about 310 to 230 BCE) proposed something bolder: the Sun at the center, with Earth moving around it. The best surviving description of his idea comes from Level 62’s Archimedes, in a book called the Sand-Reckoner. Archimedes noted the catch: if it were true, the universe would be vastly larger than anyone believed.

mascot.line: Keep this: the Sun-centered idea lost on the evidence people could see, not on stubbornness.

cards.headline: Why the Sun lost
cards.body: If Earth moves, the stars should seem to shift as you watch from different points on its path. Nobody could see any shift. Aristarchus’s answer was that the stars are immensely far away, but that meant a universe far bigger than anyone believed, and no one could test it. So the idea won little support. The Greeks weren’t being stubborn: they were following the evidence they could see.

cards.headline: Checking the old records
cards.body: In the 2nd century BCE, Hipparchus catalogued about 850 stars. Comparing his observations with ones from the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE, he found stars had shifted about 2°: the precession of the equinoxes. Old notes, compared carefully, revealed a slow drift of the stars. Around 150 CE, Ptolemy’s Almagest built on his work and kept Earth at the center.

title: The Antikythera Mechanism
objective: After this level you can describe the ancient Greek geared calculator.
summary: Found in a shipwreck in 1901, the Antikythera mechanism (about 100 BCE) used 30 surviving bronze gears to show the Sun, Moon and eclipses. Nothing as complex is known for about a thousand years.

cards.headline: In 1901, divers raised lumps of bronze from a wreck. It was a sky calculator.
cards.body: Nothing as complex survives from the ancient world. Here’s what it did.

cards.headline: A wreck full of surprises
cards.body: The mechanism came from a trading ship that sank in the first half of the 1st century BCE, off the small island of Antikythera. Sponge divers found the wreck, and in 1901 the device came up in corroded fragments. It had been made around 100 BCE, give or take 30 years. From the outside it looked like junk. The inside was another story.

cards.headline: Thirty gears inside
cards.body: X-ray images showed that the fragments hold 30 bronze gear wheels. Turn a hand crank and the gears moved pointers that showed the Sun and Moon in the zodiac, the Moon’s phases on a half-silvered ball, and eclipses to come. Think of a clock that tells you not the hour but the sky.

cards.fact: It even knew when the Olympics were due.
cards.context: The mechanism showed when the Panhellenic games, including the ancient Olympic Games, would take place. The same bronze gears predicted eclipses and kept the sports calendar.

cards.headline: A thousand years ahead
cards.body: No geared mechanism as complex is known from the ancient world, or from anywhere until medieval cathedral clocks, about a thousand years later. That’s what makes it so startling. It isn’t just old. It’s a machine nobody else managed to match for a millennium.

title: Hippocrates
objective: After this level you can explain Hippocrates’ approach to medicine.
summary: Hippocratic writers treated diseases as having natural causes, even epilepsy, the “sacred disease”, and recorded case histories. Most of the 60 writings under Hippocrates’ name aren’t by him.

cards.headline: Epilepsy was “the sacred disease.” One Greek medical book called that an excuse.
cards.body: That book belongs to a collection linked to Hippocrates. Its big idea: diseases have natural causes.

cards.headline: A name on a shelf
cards.body: Hippocrates lived from about 460 to 375 BCE and worked on the island of Cos. Plato mentions him as an admired physician and teacher, but facts about his life are hard to separate from later tales. About 60 medical writings carry his name, and most weren’t written by him. So “Hippocrates” is part man, part label on a whole shelf of Greek medicine.

cards.headline: Not sacred after all
cards.body: One of those writings, On the Sacred Disease, takes on epilepsy. Its author says it is “nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause”, and he places that cause in the brain. People who blamed the gods, he says, were using them as a screen for their own inability to cure it. Look for causes in the body, not in the heavens.

cards.headline: Natural, but not always right
cards.body: Hippocratic writers recorded case histories and cared about diagnosis and prognosis: what’s wrong, and what will happen next. Their natural explanations weren’t always correct. On the Nature of Man taught that health is a balance of four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The idea was still current in Europe’s Middle Ages. Natural, yes. Right, no.

cards.fact: The Hippocratic Oath probably wasn’t written by Hippocrates.
cards.context: It dates to about 400 BCE. Doctors swore by Apollo and other gods to give only beneficial treatment and keep patients’ secrets. Revised versions are still used at many medical school graduations.

title: The First Atoms
objective: After this level you can explain Democritus’s idea that everything is made of atoms.
summary: Leucippus and Democritus argued that everything is made of uncuttable atoms moving in the void. No one could see one to check, and Aristotle rejected the idea.

cards.headline: Cut a pebble in half. Then again. And again. Where does it stop?
cards.body: Two Greek thinkers said the cutting has to end somewhere, at a piece too small to cut. They called it the atom.

cards.headline: The uncuttable
cards.body: Leucippus and his pupil Democritus, a citizen of Abdera born about 460 BCE, built the theory. Everything, they said, is made of atoms: pieces too small to be divided, which is what the name means. Between the atoms is the void, empty space for them to move through. Atoms and void. That was the whole universe.

cards.headline: An alphabet of matter
cards.body: Atoms differ only in shape, arrangement, position and size. Water and iron differ by how their atoms are put together. Aristotle explained it with letters: A differs from N in shape, AN from NA in arrangement, and N from Z in position (turn an N on its side). A few letters make endless words. A few kinds of atoms make the world.

cards.headline: Sweet by convention
cards.body: So where do taste and color come from? Democritus put it bluntly: “by convention sweet and by convention bitter, by convention hot, by convention cold, by convention color; but in reality atoms and void.” Sweetness isn’t out there in the atoms. Only atoms and void are really there.

mascot.line: Keep this: no one could see an atom, so the whole theory stood on argument.

cards.fact: No one could look at an atom to check.
cards.context: The atoms seemed far too small to perceive, so the theory stood on argument alone. Aristotle wasn’t convinced: he rejected atomism, refusing to believe that all of reality comes down to atoms.

title: Mapping the Known World
objective: After this level you can describe Greek maps of the world.
summary: Anaximander drew the first Greek world maps on a drum-shaped Earth; Eratosthenes coined geography and drew a grid; Ptolemy listed about 8,000 places by latitude and longitude.

cards.headline: How do you map the world when you’ve only seen a slice of it?
cards.body: Greek mapmakers started with a drum-shaped Earth and ended with a grid of numbers. Here’s how the known world got drawn.

cards.headline: A world on a drum
cards.body: Anaximander of Miletus (about 610 to 546 BCE) drew a map of the known world, later corrected by his fellow Milesian Hecataeus. He pictured Earth as a squat cylinder, like a drum, one-third as thick as it is wide, held up by nothing at all. People lived on the flat top. Wrong shape, bold idea: a world that doesn’t need anything to stand on.

cards.headline: Eratosthenes draws a grid
cards.body: Remember Level 63’s Eratosthenes? He also invented geography as a subject, probably coining the word geographia itself. His Geographika placed some 400 places, from Thoule (probably Iceland) to Taprobane (Sri Lanka), on a grid of lines we’d call parallels and meridians. Now faraway places could be placed in relation to each other.

cards.headline: A world made of numbers
cards.body: In the 2nd century CE, Ptolemy’s Geography went further: it gave the latitude and longitude, in degrees, of about 8,000 places. That’s a map written as a list, so anyone could redraw it. When it was translated into Latin between 1406 and 1409, its grid gave Renaissance mapmakers a framework to fill.

title: Greek Inventions
objective: After this level you can name Greek inventions, from the water mill to the steam toy.
summary: Ctesibius improved the water clock; Hero’s aeolipile spun on steam but powered only toys; the water mill spread from Greece and freed people from grinding grain by hand.

cards.headline: The Greeks built a steam engine. They used it to spin toys.
cards.body: Other Greek machines did go to work: clocks, pumps and mills that ran on water, air and steam.

cards.headline: A clock that drips
cards.body: Ctesibius of Alexandria, working around 270 BCE, improved the water clock. Water dripped in at a steady rate and raised a float, and the float held a pointer that marked the hours. He also invented force pumps and a water organ, in which the weight of water forced air through the pipes. Time, pressure and music, all from plumbing.

cards.headline: Steam, just for fun
cards.body: More than three centuries later, around 62 CE, Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile: a sphere with two bent nozzles. Steam rushing out of the nozzles spun it round. It counts as the first steam-powered engine, and it was used to power toys and amuse visitors. His Pneumatica also describes coin-operated machines, singing birds and a fire engine.

cards.headline: The mill that freed hands
cards.body: One Greek invention truly went to work. One of the oldest references to a water mill is a Greek poem celebrating that it freed the young women who ground grain in hand mills from their toil. Easy to build and able to run in any fast stream, the water mill spread from Greece and was in use throughout Europe by the end of the 3rd century CE.

title: Checkpoint: Science and Math
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek thinkers used reason to study nature.
summary: Greek thinkers studied nature through proof, measurement and argument, looking for natural causes. Archimedes prized a proof enough to want it on his grave.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: Archimedes built war machines. His tomb showed geometry.
cards.body: That choice says a lot about how Greek thinkers ranked their work, and how they went about studying nature.

cards.headline: A sphere in a cylinder
cards.body: Archimedes proved that a sphere has two-thirds the volume of the cylinder that just holds it, and he asked for a sphere in a cylinder on his tomb. About a century and a half later, Cicero found it, overgrown with plants. According to Plutarch, Archimedes thought so little of practical inventions that he wrote nothing about them. The proof, not the machine, was the prize.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 7 together. Greek thinkers looked for natural causes, not divine ones, and trusted reasoning that could be checked: a proof, a measured angle, a star position in an old record. They got plenty wrong, from a drum-shaped Earth to the four humors. But checking was built in. Comparing old records is exactly how Hipparchus found the stars slowly drifting.

title: The Theater
objective: After this level you can describe Greek theaters and the festivals they served.
summary: Athens staged plays as contests at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of Dionysus; theaters set seats on a hillside around a round dancing floor.

cards.headline: In ancient Athens, the best seat at the play was saved for a god.
cards.body: Not for a king or a general, but for Dionysus himself. That tells you something important: a Greek play wasn’t a night out. It was a festival.

cards.headline: A holy day with a prize
cards.body: Athens staged its plays at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of Dionysus, in his theater on the south slope of the Acropolis. On festival days the god’s image was carried in from his nearby temple, so he could be present at the plays. And the plays competed: each chosen poet entered three tragedies and a satyr play, and a panel of judges picked the winner. Picture a film festival that is also a religious holiday.

cards.fact: Poor Athenians were given their theater money.
cards.context: At first, admission was free. When a charge came in later, poor citizens were handed the entrance money. Imagine your city covering your ticket because the show was part of a holy day.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize a floor plan. The words carry it: theatron, orchestra, skene.

cards.headline: A seeing place on a hill
cards.body: Greek theaters grew out of a flat patch of ground in front of a natural hill, with the audience sitting on the slope. The words still carry the floor plan. Theatron meant “a place of seeing”. The orchestra was the flat, round dancing place in the middle. Actors dressed in the skene, a small tent at the back, which gave us the word “scene”. Go “behind the scenes” and you’re in a Greek changing tent.

cards.fact: Some Greek theaters still work.
cards.context: The theater at Epidaurus was built into a mountainside in the late 4th century BCE and is famed for its acoustics. Every summer, a festival still stages ancient drama there. You can sit on the same slope and hear the same plays.

title: Tragedy
objective: After this level you can explain Greek tragedy and its great writers.
summary: Tragedy grew from a chorus to three masked actors; Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote about 300 tragedies, of which about 33 survive.

cards.headline: Three Athenians wrote about 300 tragedies. About 33 survive.
cards.body: Who were they, what did their plays look like on stage, and why did the least successful of the three end up with the most plays today?

cards.headline: One actor, then two, then three
cards.body: Tragedy started with a chorus. Tradition credits Thespis, in the 6th century BCE, as the first actor to speak apart from it; actors are still called thespians. Aeschylus added a second actor and Sophocles a third. That was the limit: never more than three speaking actors. All were men, all in masks, so one man could come back as a queen with a change of face. A chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced.

cards.headline: Stories the audience already knew
cards.body: Tragedies almost always took their plots from myth. The audience knew the outline, but not which version the playwright would tell. Aeschylus’s Oresteia, staged in 458 BCE, is the only complete Greek trilogy to survive. It opens with Agamemnon coming home from the Trojan War, and his wife, Clytemnestra, murdering him. Everyone knew the king would die. The suspense was in how.

mascot.line: Hold on to this: survival followed later fame, not prizes. Level 80 comes back to it.

cards.headline: Lose the festival, win the library
cards.body: Aeschylus wrote about 90 plays and Sophocles about 123; seven of each survive. Euripides wrote 92, and 19 survive, counting one disputed. That’s about 33 plays out of some 300. Yet Euripides won only four first prizes in his lifetime, against perhaps 24 for Sophocles. His fame grew later and eclipsed both rivals, and that’s why more of his work made it to us.

title: Comedy
objective: After this level you can explain Greek comedy and Aristophanes.
summary: Aristophanes’s Old Comedy mocked real people with fantasy and satire; Menander’s New Comedy turned to everyday life and was recovered from papyrus.

cards.headline: In 405 BCE, a prize-winning comedy sent a god to fetch a dead playwright.
cards.body: Greek comedy could laugh at anyone: politicians, philosophers, even Dionysus, the god of the festival itself.

cards.headline: Old Comedy: nobody was safe
cards.body: Aristophanes is the master of Athens’s Old Comedy. He wrote about 40 plays, and 11 survive. They mix wild fantasy with political satire aimed at real, named people. In Knights (424 BCE) he went after the powerful politician Cleon. In Clouds (423 BCE) he mocked Socrates. Picture a sketch show roasting your country’s leaders by name.

cards.headline: Jokes with a point
cards.body: In Lysistrata (411 BCE), the women of Athens and Sparta go on strike: no sex until their husbands end the Peloponnesian War. In Frogs, which won first prize in 405 BCE, Dionysus goes down to the underworld to bring back Euripides, judges a contest between him and Aeschylus, and brings back Aeschylus instead. Remember Level 72’s tragedians? Comedy was already reviewing them.

cards.fact: Menander’s best-kept comedy was printed in 1958.
cards.context: Menander (about 342–292 BCE) was the star of New Comedy, which swapped politics for everyday life: stern fathers, young lovers, scheming slaves. He wrote over 100 plays, and they were long lost. The Dyskolos, about a grumpy old man, came back from a papyrus found in Egypt. It’s the only one of his plays to survive nearly complete. Family trouble, stock characters, happy ending: sound familiar?

title: Greek Music
objective: After this level you can describe the lyre and the aulos.
summary: Greek music centered on the lyre, with its tortoise-shell sound box, and the aulos, a pair of reed pipes; Homer shows a singer performing to the lyre.

cards.headline: A blind singer took down his lyre and sang. One guest hid his tears.
cards.body: The guest was Odysseus, hearing a song about himself, in Homer’s Odyssey. For Greeks, stories came with music. So what were they playing?

cards.headline: The lyre: a tortoise that sings
cards.body: Greeks told a myth about it: the baby god Hermes made the first lyre from a tortoise shell, then stole Apollo’s cattle, and calmed Apollo by giving him the lyre. Real lyres kept the idea. The common kind had a tortoise-shell sound box, with two arms and a crossbar holding the strings. It was played alone or to accompany singing and poetry, and learning it was part of a Greek education. Its inventor, officially, was a cattle thief.

cards.headline: The aulos: pipes with bite
cards.body: Greece’s other great instrument was the aulos: a reed pipe, usually played in pairs, one in each hand. It’s often translated “flute”, but its reeds made it sound more like an oboe. Players often strapped a leather band across their cheeks. The aulos often accompanied choruses, and it played at the theater, in worship of Dionysus, at athletic contests and at drinking parties. Remember Level 71’s dancing chorus? The aulos was often its soundtrack.

cards.fact: Homer shows a singer performing to the lyre.
cards.context: In the Odyssey, the blind singer Demodocus takes his lyre from a peg at the Phaeacian feast and sings of a quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles. Odysseus, listening at the table, hides his tears. Level 6 said Homer’s poems grew out of singers performing. Here is Homer’s own picture of one.

title: Sappho and Poetry
objective: After this level you can describe Greek lyric poetry and Sappho.
summary: Lyric poetry, named for the lyre, was sung and often personal; Sappho of Lesbos was its most admired poet, though her nine books survive only in fragments.

cards.headline: The ancients called her the Tenth Muse. Only one of her poems reached us whole.
cards.body: Nine books of poems, and time kept almost none of it. The rest is being pieced together from rubbish and a mummy’s wrappings.

cards.headline: Songs for the lyre
cards.body: Remember Level 74’s lyre? It gave its name to lyric poetry, which Greeks performed to its music, and which often spoke of personal feeling. It came in two kinds: solo songs, by poets such as Sappho and Alcaeus, and songs for a chorus, by poets such as Pindar. A lyric poem wasn’t read quietly. It was sung.

cards.headline: Sappho of Lesbos
cards.body: Sappho lived about 610–570 BCE on the island of Lesbos. She wrote about love and desire, weddings and the women of her circle, and her style was admired in every age. Scholars in Alexandria later gathered her poems into nine books. That edition was lost by the early Middle Ages. Only one poem, an ode to Aphrodite, came down to us complete. It’s like knowing a singer from one full track and a box of torn lyric sheets.

cards.headline: Poems from the rubbish heap
cards.body: The rest comes from quotations by other ancient writers, and from papyrus. Many scraps were dug up at Oxyrhynchus, an ancient rubbish dump in Egypt; others had been recycled into the plaster-like wrapping of a mummy. In 2004 scholars published papyrus that almost completed her poem on old age, and in 2013 more fragments surfaced. Sappho is still arriving, one scrap at a time.

title: Sculpture
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek sculpture became lifelike.
summary: Greek statues moved from the stiff kouros to the relaxed Kritios Boy; most bronzes were melted down, so we know many through Roman marble copies and a few sea finds.

cards.headline: In 1972, two Greek bronze warriors came up from the sea off southern Italy.
cards.body: They had been lost at sea, and that’s exactly why we still have them. First, though: how did Greek statues learn to look alive?

cards.headline: From attention to at ease
cards.body: Early Greek statues stood at attention. Archaic kouroi, carved from about 615–590 BCE on, face stiffly forward, left foot slightly forward, arms at their sides. Then, just after 480 BCE, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis, the Kritios Boy, shifted his weight onto his left leg and bent his right knee. That relaxed stance is contrapposto. Weight on both feet looks like a statue; weight on one looks like a person waiting for a bus.

cards.headline: The lost bronzes
cards.body: Many famous Greek statues were bronze, and most full-size bronzes were later melted down. Polyclitus’s Spear Bearer, from about 450–440 BCE, is gone; we know it only through Roman copies. Marble is weaker than bronze, so those copies needed props, often carved as tree trunks. See a stump beside a marble god’s leg? You may be looking at a Roman copy of a Greek bronze.

cards.fact: The sea saved the Riace Bronzes.
cards.context: The two warriors were probably made in the mid-5th century BCE and spent the centuries since underwater off the coast of southern Italy, where no one could melt them down. Brought up in 1972, they are among the few full-size Greek bronzes to survive. Losing them was the best thing that ever happened to them.

title: Painted Pottery
objective: After this level you can explain black-figure and red-figure pottery.
summary: Black-figure painted black figures and scratched in details; red-figure, from about 530 BCE, flipped the scheme; prize amphorae kept black-figure for centuries.

cards.headline: Win a contest in Athens, and your prize came in a painted jar of olive oil.
cards.body: Greek pots weren’t made for museum shelves. They mixed wine, stored oil and carried prizes, and on their sides painters reinvented how to draw a body.

cards.headline: Black-figure: paint the shape, scratch the detail
cards.body: The first great style was black-figure. It began in Corinth about 700 BCE. Painters filled in each figure in black on the bare clay, then scratched fine details through the black with a sharp point. Bold silhouettes, crisp lines, and not much room for a subtle expression.

mascot.line: People mix these up. Ask one question: is it the figures or the background that’s black?

cards.headline: Red-figure: the big flip
cards.body: About 530 BCE, painters in Athens flipped the system. Now the background was painted black, and the figures were left the red of the clay. Details went on with a brush instead of being scratched. A brush curves and flows, so painters had more freedom to show bodies, movement and faces. Red-figure became the dominant style.

cards.headline: Pots with jobs
cards.body: These were working pots. A krater was a big bowl for mixing wine with water. Prize amphorae at Athens’s Panathenaic Games came full of olive oil, with Athena on one side and the contest on the other. And they kept black-figure long after other pottery dropped it: one at Harvard dates to 340–339 BCE, nearly two centuries after red-figure arrived. A trophy doesn’t chase fashion.

objective: After this level you can name the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders.
summary: Greek columns come in three orders: Doric from the mainland, Ionic from Asia Minor, and Corinthian, the latest, first seen on a monument to a Dionysia victory.

cards.headline: A Roman architect traced a column style to a grave. Basket, tile, weeds.

cards.headline: Two shores, one wooden past
cards.body: Doric and Ionic grew up at nearly the same time on opposite shores of the Aegean Sea: Doric on the Greek mainland, Ionic in the Greek cities of Asia Minor. Both began in temples built of wood. The Roman architect Vitruvius even gave them bodies: Doric was proportioned like a man, Ionic like a woman, with its scrolls like curling hair. Sturdy and plain on one shore, slender and curly on the other.

cards.headline: The basket on the grave
cards.body: Corinthian came last. Vitruvius told how a basket was left on a Corinthian girl’s grave, covered with a tile. An acanthus plant grew up around it, and the sculptor Callimachus, passing by, turned the leafy basket into a capital. Treat that as legend. The hard evidence stands in Athens: the Monument of Lysicrates, built in 334 BCE to celebrate a victory at the City Dionysia, has the earliest surviving Corinthian columns.

title: The First Historians
objective: After this level you can explain what Herodotus and Thucydides set out to do.
summary: Herodotus inquired into the Greco-Persian Wars and became the father of history; Thucydides, who lived through the Peloponnesian War, wrote it as a possession for all time.

cards.headline: “So that things done by man not be forgotten in time.”
cards.body: That’s how Herodotus opened the first great narrative history of the ancient world. Soon another Greek, Thucydides, set out to do the job differently.

cards.headline: Herodotus asks around
cards.body: Herodotus was born about 484 BCE in Halicarnassus, in Asia Minor. He called his work an inquiry: into the Greco-Persian Wars, and into their cause. He traveled widely, as far as Egypt, and wrote down the traditions people told him without vouching for all of them. That earned him the title “father of history”, and, from critics, a reputation for believing too much.

mascot.line: Don’t mix them up: Herodotus wrote down what people told him; Thucydides lived through his war.

cards.headline: Thucydides was there
cards.body: Thucydides, an Athenian, lived through the war he wrote about: the Peloponnesian War. He caught the plague that struck Athens in 430–429 BCE. As a general in 424 BCE he failed to save the city of Amphipolis and was exiled for 20 years. His history breaks off in 411 BCE, before the war was over. He wasn’t collecting old stories; he was reporting on his own lifetime.

cards.fact: Thucydides called his book “a possession for all time”.
cards.context: He admitted that the absence of romance might make it less appealing. But he wasn’t writing to win the applause of the moment, he said. In a chapter full of festival prizes, here’s a writer aiming past the judges, at you.

title: Philip of Macedon
objective: After this level you can explain how Philip conquered the Greek cities.
summary: Philip II, once a hostage in Thebes, built an army around the long sarissa, beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and was murdered in 336 BCE.

cards.headline: A hostage from Macedonia grew up to become master of Greece.
cards.body: As a young man, Philip was held in Thebes. In 338 BCE he beat Thebes and Athens in a single battle. What did he learn in between?

cards.headline: Schooled by the enemy
cards.body: Around 367 BCE, Philip, a young prince of Macedonia, was sent to Thebes as a hostage and stayed about three years. He used the time well: he studied under Epaminondas, Thebes’ great general. In 359 BCE, at 23, Philip became king of Macedonia. Imagine a rival team’s coach giving you private lessons, then sending you home.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing about Philip, make it the sarissa: his point reached you first.

cards.headline: A longer reach
cards.body: Philip rebuilt his army around the sarissa, a pike roughly twice as long as the spear other Greeks carried. Think of a shoving match where your opponent’s pole is twice as long as yours: his point reaches you before yours reaches him. Greek armies were about to find out how that felt.

cards.fact: In 338 BCE Philip beat Athens and Thebes together at Chaeronea.
cards.context: His son Alexander, only 18, commanded the left wing. Remember Level 2’s Athens and Thebes, less than 100 km apart yet foreign rivals? They finally fought side by side, and lost side by side. In 337 BCE Philip gathered the Greek states into the League of Corinth, with himself as leader, and planned a war on Persia.

cards.headline: The war he never fought
cards.body: Philip never reached Persia. In 336 BCE, during celebrations of his daughter’s wedding in the theater at Aegae, his own bodyguard Pausanias stabbed him to death. Alexander, born in 356 BCE, became king at 20. He inherited the army, the league and the plan.

title: The Education of Alexander
objective: After this level you can explain how Aristotle taught the young Alexander.
summary: From 13 to 16, Alexander was taught by Aristotle at Mieza; he treasured Aristotle’s edition of the Iliad and traced his family back to Achilles.

cards.headline: Alexander slept with a dagger and a book under his pillow.
cards.body: So Plutarch says. The book was the Iliad, in an edition prepared by his teacher. Who teaches a future conqueror?

cards.headline: The best tutor in Greece
cards.body: Philip sent for Aristotle, in Plutarch’s words ’the most famous and learned of philosophers’, to teach his son. From age 13 to 16, Alexander studied with him in a quiet school in the precinct of the nymphs near Mieza. Aristotle inspired his interest in philosophy, medicine and scientific investigation. Not a bad homeschool.

cards.headline: The tuition fee was a town
cards.body: How do you pay the most famous thinker around? According to Plutarch, Philip rebuilt Aristotle’s hometown, Stageira, and brought back its citizens from exile or slavery. The awkward part: Philip was the one who had destroyed it. Tuition, with an apology built in.

cards.headline: A soldier’s handbook
cards.body: Remember Level 6? Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education. Alexander took that further. He called the Iliad a handbook of the art of war and carried Aristotle’s edition, the ’Iliad of the Casket’, on campaign. Plutarch says his mother’s family descended from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles. For most Greek boys, the Iliad was a school text. For Alexander, it was family history.

title: Bucephalus
objective: After this level you can retell the story of Alexander's horse.
summary: Plutarch tells how young Alexander tamed Bucephalus by turning him from his shadow; the horse died in India in 326 BCE. The story comes from writers of about four centuries later.

cards.headline: Nobody could ride the horse. Then a boy noticed its shadow.
cards.body: It’s the most famous horse story in history. Here it is, and then the catch: who told it?

cards.headline: 13 talents of trouble
cards.body: Plutarch tells it like this. A horse dealer offered Philip a horse for 13 talents, a fortune. The horse was wild; no one could mount him. Young Alexander noticed the horse was frightened by his own shadow, so he turned him toward the sun, calmed him and rode off. Philip, Plutarch says, told him: ’seek thee out a kingdom equal to thyself; Macedonia has not room for thee.’

cards.headline: A horse with a city
cards.body: The horse’s name, Bucephalus, is Greek for ’bull-headed’. He carried Alexander all the way to India and died, aged 30, after the battle on the Hydaspes River in 326 BCE. Alexander named several cities Alexandria after himself. This one he named Bucephala, after his horse.

mascot.line: Same question as Level 31’s Sparta: who wrote this story, and how much later?

cards.fact: Our main accounts of Alexander were written about four centuries after he died.
cards.context: Plutarch was born around 46 CE, in Chaeronea of all places. He and Arrian drew on eyewitness histories, like one by Callisthenes, that are now lost. It’s like writing a biography today of someone who lived four centuries ago, from notes nobody can check. So treat the shadow story as a good story from a late source.

title: To India and Back
objective: After this level you can explain how far Alexander marched and why he turned back.
summary: Alexander crossed the Indus in 326 BCE and beat Porus on the Hydaspes, but his army refused to go past the Hyphasis, and the march home through Gedrosia was a disaster.

cards.headline: Alexander’s army marched all the way to India. Then, at a river, it said no.
cards.body: No enemy stopped Alexander at the Hyphasis. His own soldiers did.

cards.headline: Farther east
cards.body: After Persia came years of fighting in Central Asia. There Alexander captured Roxana, daughter of a local noble, and married her to make peace. In spring 326 BCE he crossed the Indus into India.

cards.headline: ’Like a king’
cards.body: On the Hydaspes River in 326 BCE, Alexander met King Porus, whose elephants were unfamiliar to the Macedonians. Alexander won. Asked how he wished to be treated, Porus, Plutarch says, answered: ’like a king.’ Impressed, Alexander kept him as ruler and gave him more land. The same battle cost Alexander his horse: Level 83’s Bucephalus died there.

cards.headline: The army says no
cards.body: At the Hyphasis River, the army mutinied and refused to go any farther. Alexander, Plutarch says, shut himself in his tent in anger, then gave in. He set up 12 altars to the 12 Olympian gods to mark the spot. The conqueror of Persia was stopped by his own tired men.

cards.headline: The long way home
cards.body: The way back was worse. The march through the Gedrosian desert was a disaster of thirst and hunger. Plutarch wrote that not even a quarter of the fighting force came back from India. Getting there was glory. Getting home was survival.

title: The Death of Alexander

cards.headline: Alexander conquered an empire. He never said who should get it.
cards.body: Asked on his deathbed, he may have given the most dangerous answer possible.

cards.headline: Babylon, 323 BCE
cards.body: In Babylon, Alexander fell ill after a long banquet and drinking bout. Ten days later, on June 13, 323 BCE, he died, aged 32. What killed him is still debated: malaria, typhoid fever and poison are the favorite theories. Plutarch thought the poison story a fabrication.

mascot.line: Don’t worry whether he really said it. Remember what followed: the strongest fought for it.

cards.headline: ’To the strongest’
cards.body: The historian Diodorus says the dying Alexander handed his ring to his general Perdiccas. Asked who should have his kingdom, he answered: ’to the strongest.’ Whether or not he said it, that’s exactly what happened. It’s like leaving your house to ’whoever grabs the keys first’.

cards.headline: Two kings, no king
cards.body: Alexander had named no heir, so his generals made two kings: his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his son by Roxana, Alexander IV, born after his death. Neither truly ruled. In 310 BCE the general Cassander had the boy and his mother Roxana killed. Alexander’s family was gone; his generals, the Successors, fought on until 281 BCE.

cards.fact: Alexander’s death in 323 BCE ends the Classical age.
cards.context: Remember Level 1’s timeline? The Classical age runs to his death, and the Hellenistic age begins, lasting until Rome takes Egypt in 30 BCE. One man’s death marks the border between two eras.

summary: In Greek-ruled Alexandria, the Ptolemies built a library meant to hold every book, mostly Greek, and a Greek architect built the Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders.

cards.headline: Athens lent its most precious books to a king. It never got them back.
cards.body: The borrower was building the greatest library of the Greek world, in a Greek city in Egypt.

cards.headline: All the books in the world
cards.body: About 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found a library and the Mouseion in Alexandria. Demetrius was an Athenian statesman and philosopher at Ptolemy’s court. The aim: collect, if possible, all the books in the world. Most of them were in Greek. A Greek king in Egypt, with an Athenian running the project.

cards.fact: Ptolemy III kept Athens’ official copies of its great tragedies.
cards.context: He borrowed the texts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, leaving 15 talents of silver as security. Then he kept the originals, sent back copies, and let Athens keep the silver. Think of it as the grandest unreturned library book of all.

cards.headline: A catalog in 120 books
cards.body: Finding anything among that many scrolls took a system. The scholar Callimachus, who worked at the library, compiled the Pinakes: a catalog of its authors and their works, sorted by field of learning. It filled 120 books. The catalog alone was a library.

cards.headline: A Greek light on the harbor
cards.body: Out on the island of Pharos stood the lighthouse, built by the Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidus and finished about 280 BCE. It rose more than 110 metres, with a fire burning at the top at night, and it was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

cards.headline: Pydna, 168 BCE

title: Greek in Our Words
objective: After this level you can name everyday English words that come from Greek.
summary: Telephone ("far voice"), photograph ("light writing"), school ("leisure") and dinosaur ("terrible lizard") are all built from Greek parts.

cards.headline: Telephone, photograph, school, dinosaur. You speak more Greek than you think.
cards.body: Every one of those words is built from ancient Greek parts. Take them apart and some surprising meanings fall out.

cards.headline: A far-voice in your pocket
cards.body: Start with your phone. Telephone joins two Greek words: tele, “far”, and phone, “sound” or “voice”. The word first named something else: around 1830, a system that sent words using musical notes. So every time you say “phone”, you’re saying “voice” in Greek, and a telephone is, quite literally, a far-voice.

cards.headline: Writing with light
cards.body: In 1839 the English scientist John Herschel needed a name for pictures made by light. He built one from Greek: photo-, “light”, and -graph, “something written”. A photograph is light-writing. Greek gave the new invention a name that explained exactly what it did.

cards.headline: School meant spare time
cards.body: Here’s the surprise. School comes, through Latin, from Greek skhole, which meant “leisure” or “spare time”. Leisure was what Greeks spent on learned discussion, and the word came to mean the place for it. So school began as free time well spent. Try that argument on a Monday morning.

cards.fact: Greek still names brand-new things.
cards.context: In the 1840s the anatomist Richard Owen needed a word for giant fossil reptiles. He built dinosaur from Greek deinos, “terrible”, and sauros, “lizard”. Level 8’s alphabet was built from Greek parts too: alpha plus beta.

title: Democracy Then and Now
objective: After this level you can compare ancient and modern democracy.
summary: Athenian democracy was direct but open only to adult male citizens; most modern democracies are representative, the kind of republic Madison argued suits a large country.

cards.headline: Athens called itself a democracy. So do many countries today.
cards.body: Same word, very different machine. Put the two side by side and see what changed.

mascot.line: People mix these up: Athenians voted on laws themselves; today we mostly elect people to do it.

cards.headline: Rule by the people, in person
cards.body: Democracy comes from Greek demos, “people”, and kratos, “rule”. In Athens that was meant literally: citizens voted on laws themselves in the Assembly. Most democracies today are representative: you vote for people who make the laws for you. In Athens you didn’t elect a lawmaker. If you were a citizen, you were one.

cards.headline: Who counted as “the people”?
cards.body: But “the people” was a small club. Only adult male citizens could take part; women, slaves and foreigners were shut out, so most people living in Athens had no vote. Modern democracies have widened the circle, slowly. In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let women vote in national elections.

cards.headline: Madison’s big-country problem
cards.body: The new United States faced a problem Athens never had: size. In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison described a pure democracy as a small number of citizens who assemble and govern in person. A republic, run by elected representatives, could cover a far larger country. Most modern democracies are closer to Madison’s republic than to Athens.

title: The Modern Olympics

cards.headline: The Olympics came back in 1896. Some of the oldest-looking parts were brand new.
cards.body: The revival borrowed a Greek name and a Greek stage. Then it invented traditions that look far older than they are.

cards.headline: A Frenchman’s revival
cards.body: The comeback was led by Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator. In 1894 a congress at the Sorbonne, in Paris, agreed to hold international Olympic Games and founded the International Olympic Committee. The first modern Games opened in Athens in 1896. A Greek festival, restarted by a Frenchman, back in Greece.

mascot.line: This is Level 35’s legend: the race honors a run Herodotus never recorded.

cards.headline: The newest old race
cards.body: The marathon was invented for those 1896 Games, inspired by the legend of a runner carrying news from Marathon to Athens. A Greek, Spyridon Louis, won it by more than seven minutes and became a national hero. The race that sounds most ancient was brand new, and the host country won it. Perfect ending.

cards.fact: The Olympic torch relay began in 1936, not in ancient Greece.
cards.context: It was created for the 1936 Berlin Games, staged by Nazi Germany. A flame was lit at Olympia with a mirror focusing the Sun’s rays, then runners carried it to Berlin. Ancient Greeks never ran a torch relay. It looks ancient because it was designed to.

cards.headline: Why does a bank in Philadelphia look like a Greek temple?
cards.body: Because in the 1800s, Europe and America fell hard for Greek temples, and started building them for money and memory.

cards.headline: The Greek Revival
cards.body: In the first half of the 19th century a style called the Greek Revival spread through Europe and the United States. Its architects based their designs on Greek temples of the 5th century BCE, and the Parthenon in Athens was a favorite model. For a few decades, looking ancient was the most fashionable thing a new building could do.

cards.headline: A temple for money
cards.body: The Second Bank of the United States, in Philadelphia, was built from 1819 to 1824. Its architect, William Strickland, took the Parthenon as his model, borrowing its columns and its plain pediments. An ancient temple became the template for a bank. Next time a bank greets you with a row of columns, you’re looking at a Greek temple’s descendant.

cards.headline: Democracy in stone
cards.body: The Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., dedicated in 1922, has a reason as well as a look. Its architect, Henry Bacon, modeled it on the Parthenon because he felt a memorial to a man who defended democracy should echo democracy’s birthplace. Its 36 columns stand for the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died. The shape is Greek; the count is American.

title: Myths on Screen

summary: Joyce’s Ulysses, Harryhausen’s skeletons and Percy Jackson retell Greek myths; retellers have always added details, like Achilles’ heel.

cards.headline: Books and films keep changing Greek myths. That’s a very old tradition.
cards.body: From a Dublin novel to an Olympus in a skyscraper, the old stories keep getting retold, and remixed.

cards.headline: Odysseus in Dublin
cards.body: In 1922 James Joyce published Ulysses, a novel set in Dublin on a single day, June 16, 1904. It’s built as a modern parallel to Homer’s Odyssey, with an ordinary Dubliner, Leopold Bloom, as Odysseus. The title is the Latin-based name for Odysseus. Level 6’s ten-year voyage home shrinks to one long day around town.

cards.headline: Skeletons and skyscrapers
cards.body: Films and novels do it too. For Jason and the Argonauts (1963), animator Ray Harryhausen spent four months on one stop-motion battle: Jason and two Argonauts against an army of skeletons. In Rick Riordan’s 2005 novel The Lightning Thief, Percy Jackson learns he’s a son of Poseidon, and Mount Olympus sits on the 600th floor of the Empire State Building. The gods just moved to New York.

mascot.line: Like Level 5’s wooden horse, missing from the Iliad: famous details often arrive late.

cards.headline: The heel Homer never mentioned
cards.body: Even famous details can be latecomers. The story that Thetis dipped baby Achilles in the River Styx, leaving only the heel she held vulnerable, isn’t in Homer; later tellers added it. Remember Level 6? Singers reshaped their stories every time they performed. A film that adds a twist is joining a very old habit.

title: Science's Greek Roots
objective: After this level you can name ideas in modern science that began in Greece.
summary: Science still speaks Greek: the "uncuttable" atom, Rutherford’s alpha and beta rays, and a doctors’ oath descended from Hippocrates.

cards.headline: Atom means “uncuttable” in Greek. Then physicists found its parts.
cards.body: Modern science still talks in Greek words, letters and promises, even where the science has moved on.

cards.headline: The uncuttable atom
cards.body: Atom comes from Greek atomos, “uncuttable” or “indivisible”. It named an ancient Greek idea: matter is made of tiny pieces that can’t be divided. In 1897 the English physicist J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, the first known particle smaller than an atom. The Greek name survived the discovery. We still call it the uncuttable thing, and we know it has parts.

cards.headline: Alpha, beta, radiation
cards.body: Scientists borrow Greek letters as labels. In 1899 Ernest Rutherford found that radioactive substances give off more than one kind of radiation. He named the less penetrating rays alpha and the more penetrating ones beta, after the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. That alphabet, remember, was adapted from Phoenician letters back in Level 8.

cards.headline: A promise that lasted
cards.body: Medicine kept a Greek promise. The Hippocratic oath is an ethical code attributed to the Greek physician Hippocrates, and versions of it still appear in the graduation ceremonies of many medical schools. In 1948 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Geneva, known as the oath’s modern version. The wording changed; the idea of a doctor’s public promise stayed.

title: How Greek Books Survived
objective: After this level you can explain how Arabic and Byzantine scholars saved Greek texts.
summary: Greek books survived through Byzantine copies like the Venetus A, Arabic translations such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq’s, and manuscripts carried west after 1453.

cards.headline: The oldest complete Iliad isn’t ancient. It’s about a thousand years old.
cards.body: So how did Greek books cross the centuries? Hand to hand, copy to copy, and sometimes by luck.

cards.headline: Copied in Byzantium
cards.body: The Venetus A, a Byzantine manuscript made toward the end of the 10th century CE, is the oldest complete text of the Iliad, more than 1,500 years after Homer. In the 15th century the Greek cardinal Bessarion acquired it and gave his whole collection of Greek manuscripts to Venice, where it still is. Level 6’s textbook of Greece reached us as a copy of a copy.

cards.headline: Saved in Arabic
cards.body: In 9th-century Baghdad, the scholar Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated works of Plato, Aristotle, Hippocrates and Galen from Greek. His Galen matters most: most of that doctor’s Greek manuscripts were lost, and some of his works survive only in Arabic. For those books, the original is gone and the translation is the survivor.

cards.headline: Back to the West
cards.body: In 1453 Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks, and Byzantine refugees brought more Greek manuscripts west. Scholars in Italy could now read original Greek, and older Latin translations made from Arabic versions began to look second-hand. Greek learning had travelled east and came back.

cards.headline: Math under a prayer book
cards.body: Some books survived by luck. A Byzantine copy of works by Archimedes was scraped and written over with prayers in the 13th century. A scholar spotted the faint math underneath in 1906, and modern imaging recovered it. It holds the only surviving copy of Archimedes’ Method.

title: Myths About Greece
objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like statues always being plain white.
summary: Greek sculptures were painted; the white look came from lost and scrubbed-off paint and 18th-century taste. And "Greek" is a Roman name: the Greeks called themselves Hellenes.

cards.headline: Picture a Greek statue. You probably see white marble. Its sculptor saw paint.
cards.body: Some of the most familiar ideas about Greece are later inventions. Here are two, starting with the color.

cards.headline: Painted, not plain
cards.body: Greek sculptures were painted in bright colors, a practice called polychromy. Researchers find surviving specks of pigment with infrared and ultraviolet light, then build full-color reconstructions. In 2023 a study found traces of Egyptian blue, white and purple paint on the Parthenon Sculptures in the British Museum. The marble was the canvas, not the finished look.

mascot.line: Keep this: the white statue is a later idea, helped along by people scrubbing off paint.

cards.headline: Where the white came from
cards.body: So why the white? Most of the paint simply wore away. In the 18th century the art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann linked whiteness with beauty, writing that color should play a minor part in it. And restorers sometimes removed surviving paint to restore an assumed original whiteness. The myth wasn’t only an accident: people scrubbed away the evidence.

cards.headline: They didn’t call themselves Greeks
cards.body: Second myth: the name. The ancient Greeks called themselves Hellenes. “Greek” comes from Latin Graeci, the Romans’ name for them. One theory traces it to Greeks from Graia who helped found Cumae, in Italy, where Romans first met Greeks. Cumae? That’s one of Level 9’s first colonies. Greece’s official name today is still the Hellenic Republic.

title: Why Greece Still Matters
objective: After this level you can explain why Greek ideas still shape the modern world.
summary: Shelley’s "We are all Greeks" helped rally Europe behind Greek independence; the fuller truth is that Greece borrowed, excluded and handed on as well as invented.

cards.headline: “We are all Greeks,” the poet Shelley wrote in 1822. Was he right?
cards.body: He meant that Europe’s laws, literature, religion and arts had their root in Greece. This chapter lets you test that claim.

cards.headline: A poem for a war
cards.body: Shelley wrote those words in the preface to Hellas, a poem inspired by the Greek War of Independence, which began in 1821. The poet Lord Byron went further: he went to Greece to help, died of fever at Missolonghi in 1824, and became a Greek national hero. In 1830 Greece became an independent state. Love of ancient Greece helped cheer on a modern one.

cards.headline: Not a lonely origin
cards.body: Shelley’s line leaves things out. Greece borrowed: its alphabet came from the Phoenicians. Its learning was carried by others: some of Galen’s works survive only in Arabic. And its democracy shut out women and slaves. Greece matters less as a pure fountain than as a crossroads where ideas arrived, changed and moved on.

cards.headline: You meet it every day
cards.body: Look back over this chapter. Say “school” and you’re saying “leisure” in Greek. The Olympics were reborn in Athens. Banks and memorials wear Greek columns. Films keep retelling the myths, and doctors still make a promise that began with Hippocrates. That’s why Greece still matters: you use it without noticing.
